sources.text:
[1] Croatia’s revised proposal: “A+” ceasefire
[2] This is Framework A (humanitarian), plus limited stabilization measures that make it real without forcing you to “sign away Dalmatia.”
[3] Duration: 96 hours (4 days).
 Start: 6 hours from agreement.
[4] Terms:
[5] Cease all fires at the agreed hour across Dalmatia theater.
[6] No offensive movement.
[7] You can rotate units in place and evacuate wounded.
[8] You can repair vehicles and move supplies rearward or laterally inside your existing controlled areas.
[9] No forward movement of artillery, rockets, or armor within the contact belt.
[10] Air restrictions:
[11] No fixed-wing combat flights over the zone.
[12] MedEvac flights only by notification, transponders on, pre-cleared corridors.
[13] Medical corridors with neutral verification.
[14] Immediate exchange of POW/MIA lists within 12 hours.
[15] A joint incident commission (one officer each + neutral chair) to handle violations fast and prevent one firefight from restarting the war.
[16] And here’s the key part that addresses your “trust” complaint:
 7) A formal communiqué signed by both presidents stating:
[17] “This ceasefire is humanitarian and operational in nature, and does not prejudge final status of Dalmatia.”
 So you do not “give up Dalmatia.” And I do not “legitimize Reunion administration.” We freeze the killing.

sources.path: REUNION/Emilio Financial Report September 31, 1992.docx
sources.text:
[1] Financial Report September 30th, 1992
[2] Using $1 = 5.8 RMC:
[3] Baseline ~ $500B USD → 2.9T RMC
 (500,000,000,000 × 5.8 = 2,900,000,000,000 RMC)
[4] Target ~ $400B USD → 2.32T RMC
 (400,000,000,000 × 5.8 = 2,320,000,000,000 RMC)
[5] So to “drop” from ~$500B to ~$400B in USD terms, Reunion’s GDP would be about 2.32T RMC at the same conversion rate.
[6] You wrote “now 2.4B RMC.” If that’s literal, it implies ~$414M USD GDP, which is an extinction-level collapse. I’m treating it as the obvious typo: 2.4T RMC, which equals:
[7] 2.4T RMC / 5.8 = ~$413.8B USD
[8] That lines up cleanly with your “roughly $400B” target.
[10] Ministry of Finance — Financial Situation Report
[11] As of 30 September 1992
[12] Executive summary
[13] Reunion’s GDP (USD-equivalent) has fallen from roughly $500B at the start of Donahue’s term to roughly $400–414B by end-September (≈ 2.32–2.40T RMC). The drop is driven by a war shock + confidence shock layering on top of an already strained post-Greece economy.
[14] The state has also expanded spending across most ministries while major packages (rail, ports, veterans, food stabilization, Dalmatian governance, digital modernization, security laws) create ongoing commitments. Revenues are weakening while obligations are rising — the mismatch is now the central threat.
[16] 1) Where the money is coming from (state revenue)
[17] Primary sources (typical shares):
[18] Consumption taxes (VAT/sales) — largest single stream; currently softening due to closures and reduced import volume.
[19] Customs & port fees — volatile; war risk and port insecurity sharply reduce throughput and raise insurance/handling costs.
[20] Payroll/income taxes — weakening as layoffs and shortened hours spread.
[21] Resource royalties & export duties — still strong structurally, but pressured by:
[22] disrupted logistics,
[23] price concessions demanded by buyers due to risk,
[24] and Bern treaty delivery obligations (explained below).
[25] SOE dividends / state enterprise profits — down as industry output falls and input costs rise.
[26] One-off receipts — asset sales, emergency levies, fines: politically sensitive and inconsistent.
[27] What changed since early-term baseline
[28] Revenue isn’t “gone,” but it’s becoming less collectible and less reliable:
[29] merchants and manufacturers delay payments,
[30] imports slow (hurts VAT/customs),
[31] risk premiums and hoarding distort normal trade,
[32] and informal/black-market activity expands.
[34] 2) Where the money is going (expenditure pressures)
[35] Even before the September shocks, Donahue had already signed a stack of spending and commitment bills. By late September, the biggest drains look like this:
[36] A) War + security state costs (fast-rising)
[37] Defense readiness and replacement after Dalmatia losses (spares, repairs, ammo, convoy protection, air operations).
[38] Internal security / port security driven by sabotage fears and incidents like Ploče.
[39] RNIA and counter-infiltration activity (even if not openly budgeted, it bleeds into Interior/Defense lines).
[40] B) Reconstruction and modernization commitments (large and sticky)
[41] From your enacted framework (NRIPA / RMEA / HTESA / NDIDMA / THRCRA and related):
[42] Infrastructure corridor spending (rail, roads, ports).
[43] Digital modernization (tax/customs/social systems, data centre).
[44] Housing restitution and rebuild zones (grants + capped-profit contracts).
[45] C) Social/veterans stabilization (politically unavoidable)
[46] Veterans reintegration + mental health services (VRMHSA).
[47] Retraining bridges and technical education expansion (HTESA + retraining acts).
[48] Food and staple stabilization (TFPS-GRA).
[49] Welfare/housing support scaling due to closures and household distress.
[50] D) Rail and energy industrial policy (big capex + long payback)
[51] French diesel procurement + local heavy maintenance licensing buildout (workshops, training, tooling).
[52] German electric traction package (10-year spares framework + advisors).
[53] Energy and industry expansion (including “drill/refine” approach in Curro’s push), which is high spend now, uncertain cashflow later.
[54] E) Debt service (now politically central)
[55] Existing debt servicing plus the new US loan servicing line (whatever the final schedule is in your canon) is now a confidence anchor: markets care less about your speeches than whether you can pay.
[57] 3) The Bern Treaty obligation (why it matters right now)
[58] $425M USD equivalent in rare earths/crystals/gems over 6 years starting July 1992:
[59] ~$70.83M/year of export value committed
[60] at 5.8 = ~410.8M RMC/year in external-value deliveries
[61] This hits Reunion in two ways:
[62] Hard-currency capacity: those exports can’t be redirected to earn flexible FX for imports/reserves.
[63] Fiscal capacity: the state’s tax/royalty/dividend take from that stream is effectively “spoken for” or diminished.
[64] It’s not the whole problem, but it makes the current squeeze tighter at exactly the worst time.
[66] 4) What’s causing the GDP drop (from ~$500B to ~$400B)
[67] This is the combined effect of real output loss and risk pricing:
[68] Real economy shocks
[69] War disruption in Dalmatia: ports and corridors operate below capacity; supply lines become fragile; projects pause or get destroyed.
[70] Industrial interruption: factories lose inputs, lose credit, or lose workers to mobilization.
[71] Collapse in tourism and discretionary services: immediate decline when a country looks unstable.
[72] Higher logistics costs: insurance, security, longer routing, convoy discipline costs, delays.
[73] Confidence/finance shocks
[74] Loan backlash and political fracture: raises perceived sovereign risk; tighter credit; fewer contracts; more cash-only behavior.
[75] Port legitimacy crisis (Ploče): the single worst signal for trade confidence—“can the state secure a port city?”
[76] Capital flight / hoarding behavior: people shift into hard goods and foreign currency; reduces investable capital and tax compliance.
[77] Net: even if some sectors are still producing, the economy becomes less transactable and less financeable — which is what drives a big GDP-equivalent markdown.
[79] 5) What’s not being handled well (problem areas)
[80] Execution capacity: too many big programs at once (rail + ports + digital + housing + energy + war). That’s how money leaks and timelines slip.
[81] Internal order funding vs reality: if Interior/RNIA lines don’t match the security environment, you lose the nodes and everything else becomes waste.
[82] Deficit credibility: expanded budgets + falling revenue is a recipe for either inflationary financing, arrears, or forced cuts midstream.
[84] 6) What should be prioritized to survive the deficit
[85] If Donahue wants the country to stay intact, Finance should recommend priorities in this order:
[86] Ports + fuel + medicine + spare parts (keep the state’s arteries open)
[87] Debt service discipline + transparent ring-fencing (stop the confidence bleed)
[88] War sustainment focused on logistics, not vanity procurement
[89] Only infrastructure that protects economic nodes (ports, rail chokepoints, power reliability)
[90] Targeted food stabilization to prevent riots and radicalization
[91] Pause or tranche the long-payback expansions until markets stabilize (especially anything that invites corruption or disaster risk)

[2] 1. National Infrastructure Spine Program
[3] What it is:
 Multi-year push to fix the core arteries:
[4] Ports: Reunion City, Torrental, one Dalmatian port.
[5] Roads: main industrial and rural spines.
[6] Rail: trunk corridors prepared for electrification, diesel upgrades elsewhere.

[8] Status:
[9] Moved through Parliament to presidents desk
[11] 2. Lucania Twin-Reactor “Trident” Nuclear Refit
[12] What it is:
[13] Refit and reopen the abandoned twin-reactor Lucania plant with modern safety systems.
[14] Use it as the baseload anchor for electrification and industrial growth in the north.
[15] Linked decision:
[16] Capital nuclear plant in Reunion City is paused. Land and plans reserved, but no new build until Lucania proves the model.
[17] Status:
[18] Moving forward. Policy line agreed: pause capital plant, prioritize Lucania refit. Detailed engineering and financing planning underway.
[20] 3. Rural Modernization & Food Security Act (RMFS) – Draft Bill
[21] What it is:
[22] Equipment modernization grants + cheap credit for farmers.
[23] Region-specific crop subsidies with “insurance” style reimbursements if harvests fail.
[24] State purchase of surplus crops for strategic reserves and school/military supply.
[25] Co-ops and storage (silos, cold chain) to cut waste and strengthen bargaining power.
[26] Status:
[27] Needs further planning.
[28] Internally drafted with Agriculture, not introduced in Parliament yet.
[29] Next steps: quiet consultations with farmers’ unions, co-ops, LUP, rural MPs before it goes public.
[31] 4. Land Tenure & Rural Property Modernization (Land Reform)
[32] What it is:
[33] National cadastre and title cleanup (starting in Lucania, Northern Island, Torrental hinterland).
[34] Incentives for voluntary consolidation/co-ops (scale without forced seizures).
[35] Tax pressure + incentives to force big underused estates to either modernize or partner with tenants.
[36] Status:
[37] Concept / white paper stage.
[38] Emilio has asked Agriculture to work with him; no bill text yet.
[39] This will be politically explosive if rushed – it needs precise legal work and a long rollout plan.
[41] 5. Rail Modernization & HS Trunk Line
[42] What it is:
[43] Kill steam across the network.
[44] High-speed electric corridor:
 Lucania → Steinberg → Reunion City → Torrental (southern capital)
 – prioritized for speed, reliability, and affordable mass transport.
[45] Diesel mainline/branch upgrades everywhere else (northern rural lines, Torrental hinterland, Dalmatia, fringe islands).
[46] Status:
[47] Strategic plan in development.
[48] Political direction is set (this is the model).
[49] Needs a formal 10-year National Rail Modernization Plan: exact km, costs per phase, contractor mix, and tie-in with Lucania grid timeline.
[51] 6. Government Expenditure Audit & Cuts (Confidential)
[52] What it is:
[53] Full audit of state spending to find:
[54] Dead security programs and wartime leftovers.
[55] Zombie SOEs and pointless subsidies.
[56] Vanity projects and overlapping ministries.
[57] Goal: free 2–4% of the budget over a few years to fund the infrastructure, nuclear, and rural programs without blowing the deficit sky-high.
[58] Status:
[59] Underway / For President’s eyes only.
[60] Emilio has ordered it; Finance + audit bodies are compiling.
[61] Output will be a confidential cut list for Donahue, then a public-facing “reform” package after they decide what to kill.

sources.path: REUNION/Draft Peace Instrument (Croatian Draft).docx
sources.text:
[1] Draft Peace Instrument (Croatian Draft)
[2] “Provisional Agreement on Cessation of Hostilities, Demarcation, and Twelve-Year Non-Belligerency”
 Done at Split, on 14 September 1992 (the date the ceasefire period expired)
[3] Preamble
[4] The Republic of Croatia (“Croatia”) and the State of Reunion (“Reunion”), collectively (“the Parties”),
[5] noting the expiration of the temporary ceasefire arrangement,
[6] desiring to prevent further loss of life and disruption of civilian life,
[7] and without prejudice to either Party’s political or legal positions,
 agree as follows.
[9] Article 1 — Definitions
[10] “Reunion Forces” means all armed formations, uniformed or otherwise, under Reunion command or direction, including auxiliaries and contracted security.
[11] “Croatian Forces” means all armed formations under Croatian command or direction, including territorial units and authorized auxiliaries.
[12] “Hostile Act” includes, without limitation, any discharge of a weapon, aiming of a weapon, emplacement of mines, interference with movement, seizure of property, obstruction of roads, detention of civilians, or any act that Croatia reasonably determines threatens its forces or territorial administration.
[13] “Demarcation Line” means the line described in Article 3 and Annex A.
[14] (Note: Croatia’s draft intentionally defines “Hostile Act” broadly.)
[16] Article 2 — Cessation of Hostilities
[17] Effective immediately upon entry into force of this Agreement, the Parties shall cease all offensive operations.
[18] Reunion shall ensure that no element of Reunion Forces engages in any Hostile Act against Croatian Forces or Croatian-administered authorities in the area defined by Article 3.
[19] Croatia shall ensure safe passage for Reunion Forces strictly in accordance with Article 4.
[21] Article 3 — Territorial Demarcation and Transfer
[22] Reunion acknowledges that Croatia shall assume full civil and security administration of the territory from Zadar southward to a line terminating immediately north of Šibenik, as depicted in Annex A.
[23] Reunion shall withdraw all forces, equipment, and administrative personnel from the territory described in paragraph 1 in accordance with Article 4.
[24] Upon the final verified departure of Reunion Forces from each listed municipal area (Annex A-2), Croatia’s administration shall be deemed complete in that area.
[25] (Note: Croatia’s draft frames the change as “assumption of administration,” avoiding language that implies mutual recognition of prior control.)
[27] Article 4 — Withdrawal, Safe Passage, and Non-Interference
[28] Right of Withdrawal: Reunion Forces are permitted to depart without harassment provided they comply strictly with this Agreement.
[29] No Fire on Withdrawal: Reunion Forces shall not fire upon Croatian Forces during withdrawal, for any reason, except in response to direct, immediate, and clearly identifiable lethal fire—provided that such response is proportionate and reported under Article 8 within one hour.
[30] Corridors & Timetable: Withdrawal shall occur only through the designated corridors and times listed in Annex B. Any deviation constitutes a Hostile Act under Article 1(3).
[31] Heavy Weapons:
[32] All artillery, armored vehicles, and crew-served weapons shall be moved only in declared convoys, at declared times.
[33] Convoys shall carry visible markings agreed in Annex B-3.
[34] Air & Naval Movements: Any aviation or naval movement by Reunion within 50 km of the Demarcation Line during the withdrawal period requires prior Croatian notification and acknowledgement via the joint channel under Article 8. Failure to obtain acknowledgement constitutes a Hostile Act.
[35] No Demolition/Scorched Earth: Reunion Forces shall not destroy, sabotage, or render inoperable infrastructure, depots, ports, rail assets, utilities, or public buildings. Any damage—intentional or not—may be treated as a Hostile Act pending Croatian determination.
[37] Article 5 — Twelve-Year Non-Belligerency
[38] For a period of twelve (12) years from entry into force, the Parties shall refrain from open war against one another.
[39] The obligation in paragraph 1 shall not apply in the event of a Material Breach as defined in Article 7, or where Croatia declares that Reunion has supported or facilitated armed action against Croatia by third parties.
[40] (Note: the “non-war for 12 years” promise is made conditional and easy to void.)
[42] Article 6 — Restrictions and Compliance (Croatian Safeguards)
[43] Reunion shall not:
 a. supply arms, training, intelligence, financing, or sanctuary to any force acting against Croatia;
 b. conduct propaganda or official statements inciting hostility toward Croatia;
 c. position troops, aircraft, or fires in a manner Croatia deems threatening within 30 km of the Demarcation Line.
[44] Reunion shall ensure discipline of all irregulars, veterans’ detachments, “volunteer units,” and auxiliaries. Any act by such elements may be attributed to Reunion for purposes of Article 7.
[45] Any single confirmed act of sabotage, mining, booby-trapping, or interference with transit is deemed a Hostile Act and may be deemed a Material Breach.
[47] Article 7 — Breach, Suspension, and Termination (Fickle Clause Set)
[48] Material Breach includes any of the following, as determined by Croatia acting reasonably but conclusively:
 a. any Hostile Act by Reunion Forces or attributed elements;
 b. any deviation from withdrawal corridors/timings;
 c. any weapons discharge within the withdrawal zones;
 d. any damage to infrastructure during withdrawal;
 e. any failure to report an incident under Article 8.
[49] Upon a Material Breach, Croatia may, by written notice transmitted through the channel in Article 8, immediately:
 a. suspend obligations of safe passage; and/or
 b. suspend the twelve-year non-belligerency undertaking; and/or
 c. take such security measures as Croatia deems necessary.
[50] No arbitration, mediation, or third-party determination shall be required prior to Croatia’s suspension under paragraph 2.
[51] Reunion may request consultations within 48 hours of notice; such request shall not delay any Croatian measures taken under paragraph 2.
[52] (This is the heart of the “break it over little things” design.)
[54] Article 8 — Joint Channel, Reporting, and Notices
[55] A Joint Liaison Channel shall be established immediately upon entry into force, staffed by one senior officer from each Party.
[56] Reunion shall report any incident involving weapons, movement deviations, civilian harm allegations, or infrastructure damage within one hour of occurrence.
[57] Notices under Article 7 may be transmitted by secure line, courier, or written radio message; receipt is deemed effective upon transmission.
[59] Article 9 — Observers (Optional / Conditional)
[60] Croatia may, at its sole discretion, permit limited international or neutral observers at designated crossing points listed in Annex B-2.
[61] The absence, removal, or refusal of observers shall not affect the validity or enforcement of this Agreement.
[63] Article 10 — Entry into Force
[64] This Agreement enters into force upon signature by duly authorized representatives of the Parties.
[66] Annex A — Demarcation
[67] A-1: Map reference (Zadar to immediately north of Šibenik)
[68] A-2: Municipal handover list and dates
 (Maps and exact coordinates to be attached by the Croatian General Staff Cartography Office.)
[69] Annex B — Withdrawal Corridors and Timetable
[70] B-1: Corridor routes (primary / secondary)
[71] B-2: Crossing points and inspection points (if Croatia permits)
[72] B-3: Convoy markings, spacing, and declared manifests
[74] Signatures
[75] For the Republic of Croatia: ______________________ Date: 14 Sept 1992
 For the State of Reunion: _________________________ Date: 14 Sept 1992

[2] Date: Passed July 12

[23] Evinos & Marine Pocket,
[24] “The historical continuity of the Crown and the Republic.”

[65] Maritime & Fisheries ministry lobbied hard.

sources.path: REUNION/REUNION BROADCASTING DAILY (RBD)   Morning Edition  Dateline_ Reunion City _ 13 September 1992 _ 06_00.docx
sources.text:
[1] REUNION BROADCASTING DAILY (RBD)
 Morning Edition
 Dateline: Reunion City | 13 September 1992 | 06:00
[2] “THE CLOCK IS RUNNING OUT”
[3] Ceasefire Nears Expiry as Debt Shock Ripples Through Markets; Parliament Deadlocked
[4] Reunion wakes today with two crises converging into one national test: a ceasefire in Dalmatia set to expire tomorrow night, and a sudden confidence shock after the government signed a major U.S. stabilization loan under strict conditions.
[5] With the Dalmatian front still unsettled and the Assembly unable to produce coherent emergency legislation, the country’s mood has shifted from anxiety to something sharper: fear that the state is losing control of both the battlefield and the balance sheet at the same time.
[6] CEASEFIRE ENDS TOMORROW AT 23:06
[7] The four-day ceasefire signed at 18:04 earlier this week expires 14 September at 23:06, and no extension has been announced. Government spokesmen have repeated that Reunion “seeks calm but will defend its territory,” while Croatian forces remain poised along key approaches and militia activity inside Dalmatia continues to be reported.
[8] Defense officials, speaking under attribution last night, described the strategic situation as “stable but brittle,” warning that a single large incident could trigger renewed escalation with little warning.
[9] THE LOAN THAT SHOOK THE CAPITAL
[10] The President and Finance Minister have signed a U.S. sovereign stabilization facility valued at $90 million USD (approximately 522 million RMC at the government’s stated exchange convention of $1 = 5.8 RMC).
[11] The facility carries a 12% fixed interest rate, a 3% upfront fee, disbursement by tranches, and a dedicated debt service mechanism tied to state revenues. The agreement also includes embedded monitoring and audit access, strict prohibited-use clauses, and the possibility of a later rate reduction only after extended compliance.
[12] Supporters describe the facility as a lifeline to prevent fiscal collapse and to stabilize procurement for reconstruction and basic sustainment. Critics call it a “foreign leash” imposed at the worst possible moment, arguing that signing first and seeking parliamentary settlement later has shredded confidence across political camps.
[13] FEARMONGERING OR REALITY: “DEPRESSION TALK” SPREADS
[14] The most dangerous element now is not any single clause in the agreement, but the speed at which catastrophic narratives are spreading.
[15] Across the capital’s financial district yesterday afternoon, rumors of “a coming collapse” raced faster than official explanations. Several banks tightened commercial lending windows. Importers demanded shorter payment terms. Some insurers began quietly reclassifying Dalmatian-related shipments as “high risk.” Contractors with government exposure moved to protect themselves by refusing new work unless payments were guaranteed.
[16] In the streets, the consequences were immediate.
[17] RBD has confirmed a wave of abrupt closures and “temporary shutters” among smaller retailers—especially those dependent on imported inputs or narrow cash flow—driven by three pressures at once:
[18] Credit tightening: local banks reducing exposure and demanding stronger collateral.
[19] Inventory risk: suppliers requiring faster settlement or cash, fearing currency instability.
[20] Consumer panic spending: households hoarding essentials and delaying discretionary purchases, leaving many shops with sales volatility and unusable stock.
[21] RBD has also received multiple reports of severe distress among financial professionals in the capital, including reports of suicides circulating through banker and broker networks overnight. Authorities have not released official numbers, and RBD will not repeat unverified claims. Still, the atmosphere in the district has been described by witnesses as “grim, rattled, and exhausted,” with some office buildings reducing hours and security increasing at entrances.
[22] “MOM-AND-POP IS GETTING CRUSHED”
[23] In Torrental and Steinberg, shopkeepers described the same chain reaction: customers buying staples in bulk while cutting back on everything else; distributors raising prices or requiring immediate payment; and landlords unwilling to extend rent grace periods amid uncertainty.
[24] A bakery owner in Steinberg told RBD at closing time:
 “We can still bake. Flour comes in. The problem is we don’t know what we’ll pay for it next week, and the bank is acting like I’m a gambler for asking for the same credit line I’ve had for ten years.”
[25] A hardware supplier in Reunion City put it more bluntly:
 “The state is late, the banks are scared, the wholesalers want cash, and my customers are hoarding. That’s how you kill small business without firing a shot.”
[26] PARLIAMENT: EMERGENCY SESSIONS, NO RESULTS
[27] The Assembly has convened repeated “emergency sessions” since the Dalmatian setback and the signing of the loan, but as of this morning there is still no ratified framework governing:
[28] the loan’s domestic legal standing and safeguards,
[29] emergency appropriations for war sustainment and logistics resilience,
[30] or the ruleset needed to prevent detentions and security operations from igniting political blowback in Dalmatia.
[31] Party blocs remain locked in a three-way fight:
[32] RRP institutionalists want swift ratification with guardrails to restore credibility.
[33] LUP demands social protections and opposes any mechanism that could starve civilian spending.
[34] RCA–NSF wants sovereignty limits on monitor access and maximum internal security flexibility.
[35] Behind closed doors, MPs describe the situation as “panic bargaining,” where everyone knows time is short but nobody wants to be left holding responsibility.
[36] CURRO: “THE MINISTER WHO DELIVERS,” OR “THE MINISTER WHO OVERREACHES”?
[37] Finance Minister Emilio Curro remains a central figure in the public imagination—praised by some as the only official who can “keep the state running,” condemned by others as an unelected technocrat with too much reach.
[38] Curro’s dual role—overseeing national economic policy while embedded in Dalmatian logistics—has drawn both admiration and unease. Parliament is expected to demand formal boundaries around any irregular logistics efforts and to tighten procurement channels as the loan’s oversight provisions come into force.
[39] WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
[40] Everything now points to two deadlines:
[41] Today: whether Parliament can produce any functional framework for spending triage, procurement discipline, and public reassurance.
[42] Tomorrow night: whether the ceasefire expires into renewed escalation—or into an extended pause.
[43] Until then, the markets are not waiting. Neither are the public, the ports, or the front.
[44] RBD Editorial Note: Panic can become policy if it’s allowed to spread unchallenged. Reunion requires clear numbers, clear rules, and clear leadership in daylight—before rumor does the governing for us.

sources.path: REUNION/RBDN NATIONAL REPORT — 20 AUGUST 1992.docx
sources.text:
[1] RBDN NATIONAL REPORT — 20 AUGUST 1992
[2] “Reunion at a Crossroads: Rails, Reconstruction, and Rival Power Centers”
[3] REUNION CITY — Parliament concluded an intense three-week legislative sprint today, advancing a broad package of reconstruction, transport modernization, and security bills to President Donahue’s desk. The government now faces a cluster of decisions that will shape Reunion’s post-war trajectory for years.
[5] GERMAN ELECTRIC RAIL DEAL CLEARS THE ASSEMBLY
[6] Following the earlier approval of a major French diesel procurement, the Assembly today passed the German Electric Traction Implementation Act (GETIA 1992) with a strong centrist–royalist majority.
[7] The agreement authorizes:
[8] 20 modern BR 143-series freight/mixed-traffic electrics
[9] 10 BR 112-series high-speed passenger electrics
[10] A 10-year spare-parts framework
[11] Embedded technical advisors to support electrification of the A-1 “Spine”
[12] Transport officials say the combined French–German package represents “the most significant peacetime upgrade to national rail infrastructure in half a century.”
[13] Finance analysts estimate that after both deals, approximately 150M RMC remains available under the SRRSAA modernization envelope.
[14] The Ministry of Finance declined to comment directly on delivery timelines but reiterated the government’s commitment to “building the industrial backbone of the next generation.”
[16] CURRO QUIETLY GAINS SEAT ON THE DALMATIAN CITIZENS’ COUNCIL
[17] Sources inside Lucania and Dalmatian municipal offices confirm that Finance Minister Emilio Curro has formally joined the Dalmatian Citizens’ Council (DCC) as of this week.
[18] The move, though low-profile, is seen as highly consequential.
[19] Curro, known for his technocratic but ambitious style, now sits alongside:
[20] Municipal mayors
[21] Business leaders
[22] Reconstruction representatives
[23] Selected community delegates
[24] His role gives him proximity to local networks at a time when the central government is weighing the future of Dalmatian governance under the still-unresolved DTGRA bill.
[25] Curro has publicly stated only that “Reunion’s prosperity must include Dalmatia,” but his rapid rise on the regional stage has fueled speculation about deeper political aspirations.
[27] DALMATIAN PORT REHABILITATION ACT PASSES WITH WIDE SUPPORT
[28] Also clearing Parliament today was the Dalmatian Port Emergency Rehabilitation Act (DPERA), funding repairs to:
[29] Port access roads
[30] Water and sewage infrastructure
[31] Critical loading facilities damaged during last year’s conflict
[32] Priority will go to projects with local hiring quotas and community oversight panels, a concession secured by LUP and Dalmatian MPs.
[33] Work is expected to begin within weeks.
[35] VETERANS REINTEGRATION ACT PRAISED BY ALL PARTIES
[36] The Veterans Reintegration & Mental Health Support Act (VRMHSA) sailed through the Assembly with near-unanimous backing.
[37] The law expands:
[38] Mental health care
[39] Rehab programs
[40] Job placement for returning Evinos and Marine Pocket survivors
[41] It also introduces incentives for private employers and public projects to hire veterans.
[42] The Ministry of Social Affairs called it “the most comprehensive veterans’ support legislation since the civil war era.”
[44] CONTROVERSIAL SECURITY BILL DIVIDES PARLIAMENT
[45] Far more divisive was the passage of the National Internal Security & Anti-Subversion Act (NISASA).
[46] The bill expands:
[47] Surveillance powers
[48] Pre-charge detention (up to 14 days)
[49] The legal definition of “hostile propaganda”
[50] Use of special chambers for classified evidence
[51] It passed with heavy NSF and RCA backing, while LUP and civil-liberties RRP MPs condemned the measure as “a dangerous step toward a security state.”
[52] President Donahue has not yet announced whether he will sign the bill.
[54] POLICE OVERSIGHT BILL PASSES — BUT IN WEAKENED FORM
[55] The Police Conduct, Oversight & Use-of-Force Standards Act (PCOUFSA) passed after intense debate.
[56] The final version:
[57] Establishes national standards
[58] Requires reporting of custody deaths
[59] Creates internal affairs units
[60] However, proposals for an independent civilian watchdog were stripped out during committee review.
[61] Civil society groups called the result “a compromised reform.”
[63] FOOD PRICE STABILIZATION ACT ADVANCES AMID INFLATION PRESSURES
[64] The Temporary Food Price Stabilization & Grain Reserve Adjustment Act passed 19 August, authorizing short-term interventions to smooth sharp rises in staple food prices.
[65] Inflation remains elevated, with the RMC now valued at 5.8 USD compared to roughly 3 USD before the Evinos War.
[66] The Finance Ministry insisted the program is “fiscally limited and temporary.”
[68] DONAHUE’S APPROVAL REMAINS HIGH — BUT PUBLIC WATCHING SECURITY TENSION
[69] A new RBDN/University of Reunion poll shows:
[70] President Donahue approval: 61%
[71] Finance Minister Curro: 58%
[72] King Zo III: 52% (up significantly since mid-July)
[73] Field Marshal Hartmann: 47%, with hard nationalist support stabilizing
[74] Political analysts warn that Donahue’s coming decisions on NISASA, DTGRA, and GETIA will sharply define the next phase of his presidency.
[76] AN ECONOMY IN REBUILDING
[77] The Ministry of Finance’s mid-quarter report places national GDP at 18–20 billion RMC, with a deficit “slightly above 3%” due to reconstruction and training programs.
[78] Consumer confidence has slowly improved since the chaotic spring months, though households remain sensitive to rising food and energy prices.
[80] PUBLIC MOOD: CAUTIOUS OPTIMISM
[81] Despite lingering tension between royalist, nationalist, and centrist factions, the tone in Parliament this week suggests a political class aware that the country is exhausted with crisis.
[82] “The machinery of the state is moving again,” one senior RRP figure told RBDN.
 “Reunion needs normalcy, and we are trying—however imperfectly—to deliver it.”
[85] GEOPOLITICS
[87] CROATIAN TROOP BUILDUP ALONG DALMATIAN BORDER RAISES REGIONAL CONCERNS
[88] Reunion Government Calls for “Calm but Firm Vigilance” as Tensions Rise
[89] RBD – DALMATIA / REUNION CITY
 A surge of Croatian military activity along the contested Dalmatian frontier over the past ten days has triggered renewed fears of instability in the Balkans. The Reunion Ministry of Defense confirmed this week that multiple Croatian brigades have been observed moving toward the border, accompanied by stepped-up artillery drills and what officials described as “concerning provocations.”
[90] Second Brigade Confirmed in Forward Areas
[91] Satellite imagery and reconnaissance flights have verified the deployment of a second full Croatian brigade to staging positions opposite Reunion-held territory. Analysts say this represents the largest Croatian troop concentration near the border since 1991, when Reunion first intervened in Dalmatia during the Yugoslav collapse.
[92] Defense officials, speaking publicly for the first time, stated:
[93] “The movement of two brigades, supported by mechanized assets and artillery, constitutes a significant escalation.”
[95] ARTILLERY SHELLS LAND IN NO MAN’S LAND
[96] Residents and local garrisons report that Croatian artillery exercises in recent weeks have resulted in several shells landing within uninhabited areas of no man’s land inside Dalmatia.
 No injuries were reported, but the government has issued an official protest, calling the incidents “reckless and destabilizing.”
[97] Reunion forces in Dalmatia have been instructed to maintain strict fire discipline and avoid any action that could be construed as escalation.
[99] REUNION ATTACK HELICOPTER SHOT DOWN DURING BORDER INCIDENT
[100] On August 11th, a Reunion Lynx attack helicopter was shot down during what the military described as a routine patrol inside Reunion-administered territory. The incident occurred less than two kilometers from the front line.
[101] Croatia has claimed the shoot-down was an “accident” during a training exercise. Reunion’s Ministry of Defense disputed this, saying radar and flight data “strongly indicate a deliberate engagement.”
[102] The crew’s condition has not yet been released.
[104] UNIFIED DALMATIAN FRONT (UDF) ACTIVITY INCREASES
[105] Reports of Heavy Weapons & Tanks Among Militia Groups
[106] Internal security sources confirmed a rise in activity by the Croatian-aligned Unified Dalmatian Front (UDF), a coalition of nationalist militias operating inside the disputed region.
[107] Key developments now publicly acknowledged:
[108] UDF cells have distributed propaganda pamphlets urging resistance, including messages such as “Reunion will bleed dry” and “They will flee like the Soviets from Afghanistan.”
[109] Reconnaissance patrols spotted UDF fighters accompanied by armored vehicles, including what appeared to be T-72 tanks, near remote border crossings with Bosnia and Croatia.
[110] Several sabotage attempts against supply convoys and isolated outposts have been recorded in the past two weeks, though without casualties.
[111] Officials emphasized that while UDF activity remains “limited and sporadic,” the presence of heavy weapons in militia hands represents a new phase of the conflict.
[113] CARGO SHIP SEIZED WITH SMUGGLED WEAPONS
[114] The government publicly confirmed that earlier this month, Reunion naval authorities intercepted a Croatian-registered cargo ship entering a Dalmatian port under the guise of delivering construction materials.
[115] A search uncovered:
[116] Anti-tank guns
[117] Recoilless rifles
[118] Heavy machine guns
[119] Ammunition crates believed destined for UDF fighters
[120] Reunion has filed a diplomatic complaint with Zagreb, calling the act “a blatant attempt to destabilize the region through covert supply of militants.”
[121] Croatia has not officially commented on the discovery.
[123] STATE OF REUNION FORCES IN DALMATIA – GOVERNMENT RELEASES SUMMARY
[124] In response to rising public concern, the Ministry of Defense released a limited overview of Reunion’s current posture in Dalmatia.
[125] Key points:
[126] The 3rd Infantry Regiment (3,500 troops) remains the primary garrison force, supported by armored, air defense, and artillery detachments.
[127] The 2nd Armored Angels Regiment (5,000 troops) is on operational standby, equipped with a small number of Abrams tanks and light armor.
[128] Reunion air forces maintain a presence in the theater, including fighter squadrons, jamming aircraft, and attack helicopters.
[129] The government acknowledged that air defense networks are “recovering” from earlier damage sustained during the conflict in Greece.
[130] Officials reiterated that sea supply lines remain secure, thanks to the strong presence of the Reunion Navy in the Adriatic.
[132] GOVERNMENT RESPONSE: “NO INTENTION OF ESCALATION, BUT WE WILL DEFEND OURSELVES”
[133] The Foreign Minister of Reunion, addressing reporters outside the Assembly, stated:
[134] “Reunion seeks no war with Croatia.
 But we will not be intimidated, and we will not abandon the people of Dalmatia to militias or chaos.”
[135] Opposition parties are divided:
[136] The National Security Front (NSF) has accused Croatia of preparing for “a correction operation” aimed at seizing territory by force.
[137] The Labour Unity Party (LUP) called for urgent international mediation to prevent escalation.
[138] The Royalist Crown Alliance (RCA) urged a “measured but strong” response and condemned the smuggling incident.
[139] France and the United States have been briefed privately, though no foreign government has yet issued a formal statement.
[141] REGIONAL OUTLOOK: EXPERTS WARN OF POSSIBLE LATE-YEAR OFFENSIVE
[142] Military analysts interviewed by RBD believe the situation could deteriorate if Croatia continues to mass forces during the coming months.
[143] A former general familiar with the theater commented:
[144] “This isn’t posturing anymore.
 When two brigades move, artillery ranges your supply lines, and militias show up with T-72s, someone is shaping the battlefield.”
[145] Reunion security sources echoed this assessment, saying that Croatia may be preparing for a limited winter or spring offensive designed to reclaim key cities and logistics hubs in the Dalmatian strip.
[146] For now, Dalmatian residents live under the tension of an uneasy calm — a calm that many fear may not last.

[1] 20 AUG – 5 SEP 1992: EVENTS LOG
[2] 20–22 AUGUST: THE SIGNINGS LAND, THE SYSTEM LURCHES
[3] 20 Aug (Thu)
[4] Donahue signs the full stack: DPERA, SRRSAA, VRMHSA, NISASA, PCOUFSA, DTGRA, TFPS-GRA, GETIA 1992.
[5] Ministries issue “Implementation Directives” within 24 hours. Every committee chair in Parliament immediately schedules oversight hearings.
[6] 21 Aug (Fri)
[7] Interior issues the first NISASA implementing circular: defining “hostile propaganda,” detention paperwork rules, and how cases route into National Security Chambers.
[8] Justice quietly publishes interpretive guidance to judges (very conservative wording, trying to avoid legal anarchy).
[9] 22 Aug (Sat)
[10] Dalmatian ports begin DPERA “Phase 0” work: emergency road patching, crane inspections, water/sewage priority repairs.
[11] Panic buying in Dalmatian coastal towns accelerates. Inland relatives receive a visible flow of short-term evacuees “just for a few weeks.”
[13] 23–27 AUGUST: NISASA’S FIRST TESTS, DALMATIA’S FIRST CONTRACTS
[14] 23 Aug (Sun)
[15] First public NISASA enforcement operation: several arrests framed as “subversion network coordination.” The government does not name the networks; opposition media fills the vacuum with speculation.
[16] 24 Aug (Mon)
[17] Parliament reconvenes for the first post-signing session. The chamber is loud and ugly:
[18] LUP demands immediate limits on detention conditions and court secrecy.
[19] NSF and RCA hammer “deterrence” and “war readiness.”
[20] RRP tries to reframe the week as “reconstruction first, security bounded.”
[21] 25 Aug (Tue)
[22] First DPERA tenders are published. Local Dalmatian contractors surge in registration.
[23] A minor scandal breaks: one contractor appears linked to a known Dalmatian smuggling family. It’s not proven illegal—just politically radioactive.
[24] 26 Aug (Wed)
[25] Small UDF-style sabotage: a roadside culvert on a supply route is blown at night. No casualties; convoy rerouted.
[26] Government announces stricter convoy protocol and “non-negotiable fire discipline” for troops.
[27] 27 Aug (Thu)
[28] Mood in the capital splits:
[29] “The state is moving again” vs “the state is turning into a machine that can’t be stopped.”
[31] 28–31 AUGUST: DTGRA TURNS INTO A KNIFE FIGHT
[32] 28 Aug (Fri)
[33] DTGRA implementation begins. The central government requests candidate lists for the 40% appointed seats.
[34] Dalmatian municipal leaders start lobbying openly for “local legitimacy” and “no parachuted appointees.”
[35] 29 Aug (Sat)
[36] Croatian artillery “exercises” intensify. More rounds land in no man’s land. Still no direct casualties, but the psychological impact is heavy.
[37] Dalmatian local radio warns of fuel shortages even when depots remain stocked—driving more hoarding.
[38] 30 Aug (Sun)
[39] A publicized “humanitarian convoy” from a Croatian-linked NGO attempts to cross into the zone. Reunion turns it back citing security screening requirements.
[40] Croatia denounces it as obstruction; Reunion frames it as “covert supply potential.” The propaganda battle becomes constant.
[41] 31 Aug (Mon)
[42] A Dalmatian port work slowdown occurs (unofficial, a few hours), driven by fear of escalation and rumors of incoming shelling.
[43] The government urges calm and promises security, but avoids promising timelines.
[45] 1–3 SEPTEMBER: THE “THREE FRONTS” WEEK
[46] This is where Reunion gets pulled into three simultaneous conflicts: security legitimacy, Dalmatian governance, and economic anxiety.
[47] 1 Sep (Tue)
[48] TFPS-GRA visibly dampens food price spikes in Reunion City and Torrental, but retailers complain of uncertainty.
[49] Farmers’ associations begin organizing against “export restrictions,” calling it market interference.
[50] 2 Sep (Wed)
[51] First high-profile legal challenge to a NISASA detention reaches the courts. It becomes a national media spectacle.
[52] Civil-liberties lawyers accuse Interior of “testing the boundaries of lawful detention.” Interior says the case involves “active hostile coordination.”
[53] 3 Sep (Thu)
[54] A major Dalmatian incident: an IED attack hits a road crew working on DPERA-linked repairs.
[55] Limited casualties (usually 1–3 dead, several wounded) and the story explodes.
[56] Immediate consequence: road works pause for 24–48 hours; security escorts become mandatory.
[57] This is the first moment where reconstruction visibly collides with insurgency tactics.
[59] 4–5 SEPTEMBER: THE NATIONAL MOOD HARDENS
[60] 4 Sep (Fri)
[61] Parliament pushes emergency committee hearings on:
[62] Contractor vetting
[63] RIA conduct rules
[64] Compensation for affected families
[65] Whether Dalmatia should be treated as “civil reconstruction” or “counterinsurgency theater”
[66] LUP demands stronger civilian safeguards; NSF demands broader authority and faster detention powers in-theater; RRP tries to keep the coalition from splitting; RCA publicly supports “discipline and legitimacy” simultaneously (which is easy to say and hard to execute).
[67] 5 Sep (Sat)
[68] In Dalmatia, you see the most telling shift: fewer public demonstrations, more quiet behavior changes.
[69] Shop shelves cycle faster.
[70] Bus stations are crowded.
[71] People speak less freely in cafés.
[72] Nationalists become more confident in passive intimidation.
[73] In Reunion City, the mood becomes:
[74] “We’re rebuilding”
[75] “We’re being watched”
[76] “Dalmatia could drag us back into war.”
[78] Summary of What Changed by 5 September
[79] Dalmatia
[80] Reconstruction started, but the first serious attack on a reconstruction-linked target forces “security-first reconstruction.”
[81] DTGRA implementation becomes the central political battleground: appointments and legitimacy matter more than the law text.
[82] Security / Civil Liberties
[83] NISASA is no longer theoretical. By early September it has:
[84] real detainees
[85] real court challenges
[86] real media polarization
[87] Every future scandal will hit Donahue directly, even if Interior is the implementer.
[88] Economy
[89] TFPS-GRA reduces price panic, but creates a new political fault line: producers vs consumers, and “temporary stabilization” vs “permanent controls.”
[90] Rail procurement becomes a symbol: modern future vs debt and foreign dependence.
[91] RBDN SPECIAL REPORT — DALMATIA DESK
[92] 20 August 1992
 CROATIAN BUILDUP, HELICOPTER SHOOTDOWN, AND REUNION’S FORCE SURGE SHAKE DALMATIA
 Panic buying spreads in coastal towns as government urges “calm but firm vigilance”
[93] DALMATIA / REUNION CITY — A sharp rise in Croatian troop activity along the Dalmatian frontier, paired with a deadly air-defense incident on 11 August, has pushed Reunion-held Dalmatia into its most tense posture since the 1991 intervention. The Ministry of Defense confirmed that additional Croatian brigades have moved into forward staging areas opposite Reunion territory, accompanied by stepped-up artillery drills and a marked increase in militia activity inside the disputed strip.
[94] The same week, Reunion authorities ordered a significant reinforcement into theater—8,500 additional troops, including heavier armored elements and jet support—after what officials describe as a deliberate engagement against a Reunion helicopter operating within Reunion-administered territory.
[95] The result, across Dalmatian towns, is a rapid shift in civilian behavior: panic buying, inward migration, and a brittle public mood.
[97] Border posture hardens after August 11 shootdown
[98] The Ministry of Defense stated that a Reunion Lynx helicopter was shot down on 11 August during what it called a routine patrol inside Reunion-administered territory, less than two kilometers from the front line. Croatia has described the incident as an accident during training; Reunion disputes this, citing flight tracking and radar data that “strongly indicate deliberate engagement.”
[99] Officials have not publicly released the crew’s condition.
[100] In the days following, defense authorities expanded air and ground coverage, citing the need to prevent a “correction operation” against Reunion supply lines and urban nodes.
[102] Artillery “exercises” spill into no man’s land
[103] Local garrisons and residents have reported Croatian artillery rounds landing in uninhabited areas of no man’s land inside Dalmatia. No casualties were reported, but the Foreign Ministry filed a formal protest describing the incidents as reckless. Reunion forces have been instructed to maintain strict fire discipline to avoid escalation.
[105] UDF activity escalates: propaganda, sabotage, and heavy weapons sightings
[106] Internal security sources confirm increased activity by the Unified Dalmatian Front (UDF), a Croatian-aligned nationalist militia umbrella.
[107] Publicly acknowledged developments now include:
[108] Distribution of propaganda leaflets urging resistance with slogans such as “Reunion will bleed dry” and “They will flee like the Soviets from Afghanistan.”
[109] Reconnaissance sightings of UDF elements accompanied by armored vehicles—including what were described as T-72 tanks—near remote crossings and back routes.
[110] Multiple attempted disruptions of supply convoys and isolated outposts over the last two weeks, largely without casualties.
[111] Security officials describe the activity as “limited and sporadic,” but say the appearance of heavier systems in militia hands represents “a new phase of the conflict.”
[113] Smuggling incident deepens diplomatic crisis
[114] The government publicly confirmed interception of a Croatian-registered cargo ship entering a Dalmatian port under the guise of construction delivery. A search uncovered anti-tank guns, recoilless rifles, heavy machine guns, and ammunition believed destined for UDF networks.
[115] Reunion filed a diplomatic complaint in Zagreb, calling the operation a deliberate destabilization attempt. Croatia has not issued a formal public response.
[117] Civil sentiment: fear, fatigue, and fragile confidence
[118] RBDN reporting from coastal districts indicates civilian confidence remains brittle after the force surge.
[119] Current trend (as of this week)
[120] General mood: war fatigue and fear of renewed fighting; people assume “something bigger” may be coming.
[121] Panic behavior: widespread hoarding of bread staples, fuel canisters, and bottled water; families moving children inland toward relatives.
[122] Support base: port workers, merchants, and pragmatic locals show cautious relief due to increased naval and air presence—“better Reunion than chaos.”
[123] Neutral/autonomist bloc: growing anxiety; reduced cooperation with authorities due to fear of retaliation and uncertainty about long-term control.
[124] Pro-Croat nationalists: outward calm but rising passive hostility; increased likelihood of low-level sabotage and attempts to provoke security incidents.
[125] Key risk flagged by multiple local leaders: heavy-handed detentions or abusive policing could unify fence-sitters against Reunion and hand UDF a propaganda victory.
[127] Public order risk factors: next 30–60 days
[128] Security sources and municipal leaders describe several likely triggers:
[129] Likely triggers
[130] Curfews and checkpoints that disrupt commerce
[131] High-profile detainee abuse allegations or “disappearances”
[132] Fuel or bread shortages caused by convoy disruption or hoarding
[133] Likely indicators already being watched
[134] Sudden queues and hoarding behavior
[135] Civilian migration inland
[136] Increased graffiti, leaflets, work slowdowns at ports and road crews
[138] Logistics reality: sea strong, land fragile
[139] Authorities continue to express confidence in sea supply lines. Naval coverage has kept maritime resupply stable and deters overt Croatian interdiction.
[140] Land logistics remain the weak point, with vulnerabilities including:
[141] Poor roads with predictable chokepoints
[142] An older mixed truck fleet with uneven maintenance and parts scarcity
[143] Slow convoy speed and inconsistent convoy discipline
[144] Depot-centric stockpiles vulnerable to sabotage
[145] Several Dalmatian municipal officials warn that if land convoys are repeatedly disrupted, panic buying could become a self-fulfilling supply crisis.
[147] “Low-cost, high-impact” mitigations now being pushed
[148] Without announcing a full public plan, Defense and Interior officials have indicated practical steps are being prioritized:
[149] Dispersing fuel/ammo into multiple small concealed dumps rather than a few large depots
[150] Standardizing convoy schedules, escort requirements, and quick-reaction protocols
[151] Tightening RIA conduct rules to prevent political blowback:
[152] mandatory reporting for detentions
[153] stricter supervision at checkpoints
[154] stronger documentation expectations where feasible
[155] Prioritizing repairs to 2–3 critical road routes, bridges, and chokepoints
[156] Analysts note the central paradox: increased militarization improves deterrence but also increases “occupation stress.” Stability will depend less on force presence than disciplined security conduct and reliable civilian supply.
[158] Political reactions split along predictable lines
[159] NSF: calls the Croatian buildup proof of an impending “correction operation” and presses for firmer internal security measures.
[160] LUP: urges urgent international mediation and warns that abuse scandals would collapse Dalmatian cooperation.
[161] RCA: backs a measured but strong response and emphasizes sovereignty and deterrence.
[162] RRP: focuses on maintaining legitimacy through reconstruction delivery, warning privately that “force without services” is a losing formula.
[163] France and the United States have been briefed privately; neither has issued a formal statement at this time.
[165] Regional outlook: “Someone is shaping the battlefield”
[166] Analysts interviewed by RBDN warn the pattern is consistent with preparation for a limited future offensive: brigade movement, artillery ranging, militia heavy weapons, and covert smuggling routes.
[167] For now, Dalmatian residents live under what one mayor described as “an uneasy calm”—a calm that, after August 11, many no longer trust.
[168] If you want, I can produce the next-day parliamentary session coverage (Aug 21) showing exactly how RRP, LUP, NSF, RCA, and the Dalmatian MPs weaponize this situation on the Assembly floor—soundbites, interruptions, committee threats, the whole thing.

[1] REUNION ORDER OF BATTLE – DALMATIA (UPDATED 11 AUG 1992)
[2] A. Ground Forces – In-Theater
[3] 1. 3rd Infantry Regiment (3,500 troops)
[4] Status: Forward deployment in coastal and inland defensive sectors.
 Quality: Well-trained, no combat experience.
 Morale: Moderate; shaken by recent shelling and helicopter shoot-down.
 Composition:
[5] 3 × Infantry Battalions
[6] Each with rifle companies equipped with mix of FAMAS rifles & older NATO small arms.
[7] Light AT teams (LAWs, some RPG-7s captured or purchased cheaply).
[8] Mortar platoons (60mm & 81mm).
[9] Regimental Support
[10] 9 × US-made 1980s APCs (M113-derivatives; functional but aging).
[11] 6 × Field Artillery Guns (likely 105mm or 122mm equivalent).
[12] 12 × AAA pieces (old-school autocannons; insufficient vs modern aircraft).
[13] Transport trucks (logistics backbone, vulnerable to interdiction/sabotage).
[14] Capabilities:
[15] Static defense.
[16] Light maneuver along coastal roads.
[17] Limited cross-country mobility.
[18] Cannot sustain heavy armor confrontation without assistance.
[20] 2. 2nd Armored Angels Regiment (5,000 troops)
[21] Status: Held as operational reserve in central Dalmatia.
 Quality: Good training; mixed combat experience (some Evinos vets in staff).
 Morale: High but concerned about equipment issues.
[22] Key Equipment
[23] Armor
[24] 4 × M1A1 Abrams tanks
[25] Poorly maintained.
[26] Spare parts scarcity; reverse-engineered components failing early.
[27] Fire control and optics reliability down ~30–40%.
[28] Mobility acceptable; armor still formidable.
[29] 15 × Light Tanks (1970s–80s vintage)
[30] Likely AMX-13, Vickers Mk3, or similar class.
[31] Good for fire support; useless against modern Croatian T-55/T-72 fleets.
[32] Mechanized / Motorized
[33] 20 × APCs (mix of M113s & domestic light armor)
[34] 60 × Troop Transports (soft-skin trucks)
[35] Capabilities:
[36] Best armored punch Reunion can field in Dalmatia.
[37] Capable of limited counterattacks, but logistics & maintenance reduce staying power.
[38] Vulnerable if Croatian artillery pins them before maneuver.
[40] B. Air Assets – Assigned to Dalmatia AO
[41] 1. Fighters – 28 total
[42] Breakdown (assumed):
[43] 18–20 front-line fighters (Mirage III/V? F-5? F-16 early blocks if acquired from US?).
[44] 8–10 older interceptors.
[45] Condition:
 Good pilots, aviation fuel constrained, SAM radar coverage degraded.
[46] 2. CAS Aircraft – 5
[47] Light attack craft (Alpha Jets, A-37s, or domestic equivalents).
[48] Effective for counter-insurgency, vulnerable to Croatian AA.
[49] 3. Jamming Aircraft (French) – 2
[50] Critical strategic assets.
[51] Used sparingly due to maintenance concerns.
[52] Needed to degrade Croatian artillery targeting and disrupt UDF radios.
[53] 4. Attack Helicopters – 8 (Lynx-type)
[54] Current readiness: 7, after one shot down 11 Aug.
 Capabilities:
[55] Excellent anti-armor ambusher.
[56] Vulnerable at medium altitude.
[57] Requires secure forward arming and refueling points (FARPs).
[59] C. Ground-Based Air Defense & Radar
[60] Domestic SAM network at ~20% strength.
[61] Many radars destroyed or degraded from Soviet SEAD earlier in 1992.
[62] Coverage gaps across:
[63] Inland valleys,
[64] Dalmatian mountain approaches,
[65] Rear-area bridges.
[66] Current effect:
 Croatian fighters or drones can probe at will unless your fighters intercept.
[68] D. Logistics Summary
[69] Ports secure thanks to Reunion Navy.
[70] Overland logistics: weak, vulnerable to:
[71] Bridge destruction,
[72] Ambushes,
[73] Mortar attacks on supply nodes.
[74] Fuel & ammo stockpiles:
[75] Poorly dispersed.
[76] Lightly guarded.
[77] High sabotage risk.
[79] II. ASSUMED CROATIAN OOB – AUG 11, 1992 (RNIO ESTIMATE)
[80] 1. Deployed to Dalmatian Border (Confirmed)
[81] Croatian Brigade #1 (Deployed early August)
[82] 2–3 Infantry Battalions (combat experienced; some fought Serbs recently)
[83] 1 Mechanized Company (BTRs, BMP-1s, or M-80 Yugoslav IFVs)
[84] 1 Recon Company
[85] Artillery Battalion
[86] 122mm and 152mm towed artillery
[87] ~12–18 tubes
[88] Possibly 122mm MRLs
[89] Croatian Brigade #2 (Detected 11 August – Moving into Position)
[90] Likely composition:
[91] 2 infantry battalions
[92] 1 tank company (T-55s, possibly a handful of T-72s rotated from other fronts)
[93] 1 artillery battery
[94] Engineers for mine-laying and breaching
[96] 2. UDF (Unified Dalmatian Front) – Updated Assessment
[97] Strength:
 Estimated 1,500–3,000 fighters dispersed across the interior.
[98] Equipment:
[99] Small arms.
[100] RPGs.
[101] 60/82mm mortars.
[102] New intel: Presence of T-72s (captured, smuggled, or covert Croatian delivery).
[103] Likely roles:
[104] Border harassment
[105] Sabotage
[106] Anti-armor ambushes
[107] They are preparing coordinated movements with Croatian regulars.
[109] III. RNIO INTELLIGENCE BRIEF – 11 AUGUST 1992
[110] CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET – EYES ONLY
 To: President Donahue, General Hartmann, Joint Military Staff
 From: RNIO – Dalmatian Desk
 Time: 11 AUG 1992, 21:45
[112] SUBJECT: Escalating Croatian Military Activity, UDF Mobilization & Reunion OOB Review
[114] 1. NEW EVENTS – 11 AUG
[115] A. Croatian Forces Shot Down Reunion Lynx Attack Helicopter
[116] Incident occurred inside our territory near the Brac–Makarska sector.
[117] Croatian statement (radio intercept):


 “Training fire impacted unidentified aircraft. No hostile intent.”
[118] This is false.
 Trajectory and radar logs confirm a deliberate engagement, likely from a MANPADS team embedded with their forward companies.
[119] Implication:
 Croatia is willing to use lethal force preemptively while hiding behind “accident” framing.
[121] B. Second Croatian Brigade Identified Moving to Border
[122] Satellite cues + SIGINT indicate:
[123] HQ vehicles,
[124] 2 infantry battalion columns,
[125] 1 tank company,
[126] Artillery battery following via mountain road.
[127] Arrival estimated within 48–72 hours.
[128] This matches pre-offensive staging doctrine.
[130] C. UDF Armored Presence (T-72s)
[131] Reliable spotting by recon drone & QRF patrol:
[132] At least 2 T-72s,
[133] Possibly 1–2 more concealed in a farm complex.
[134] Located near the tri-border area (Bosnia/Croatia/Reunion zone).
[135] Assessment:
 These are not militia-acquired; delivery is state-supported.
[137] D. Smuggling Incident – Construction Ship
[138] Debrief of detained crew confirms:
[139] Orders came from Croatian Ministry of Defense intermediaries.
[140] Cargo included:
[141] AT guns, heavy machine guns, recoilless rifles, mortar rounds.
[142] Intended recipients:
[143] UDF cells in Split hinterland and coastal towns.
[144] Implication:
 Croatia is preparing the battlefield for a hybrid escalation.
[146] 2. RNIO THREAT ASSESSMENT
[147] Croatia’s Strategic Angle
[148] Zagreb is shaping the situation for a limited offensive (COA-2) by late 1992 or early 1993.
[149] Indicators:
[150] Two brigades massed on frontier.
[151] Artillery range-finding under guise of “exercises.”
[152] Increased UDF activity + armored elements.
[153] Direct engagement of Reunion aircraft.
[154] Their objective is likely:
[155] Territorial rollback of our coastal holdings,
[156] Fragmentation of our logistical axis,
[157] Forcing political concessions or withdrawal.
[159] 3. REUNION OOB (DALMATIA) – AUG 11, 1992
[160] (Summarized for staff use)
[161] 3rd Infantry Regiment – 3,500
[162] 3 infantry battalions
[163] 9 APCs
[164] 6 artillery guns
[165] 12 AAA guns
[166] Light AT assets
[167] Morale moderate
[168] 2nd Armored Angels Regiment – 5,000
[169] 4 × M1A1 Abrams (poor maintenance state)
[170] 15 × Light Tanks (1970s–80s)
[171] 20 APCs
[172] 60 transports
[173] High morale, moderate readiness
[174] Air Assets
[175] 28 fighters
[176] 5 CAS
[177] 2 French ECM aircraft
[178] 8 attack helicopters → now 7
[179] Ground-Based Air Defense
[180] Domestic SAM/Radar at ~20% capability
[181] Logistics
[182] SLOC safe
[183] Overland routes fragile
[184] Fuel/ammo depots weakly defended
[186] 4. ASSUMED CROATIAN OOB – AUG 11
[187] Brigade #1
[188] 2–3 infantry battalions
[189] Recon company
[190] Mechanized company
[191] Full artillery battalion (122/152mm, possibly MRLs)
[192] Brigade #2
[193] 2 infantry battalions
[194] 1 tank company (T-55/T-72 mix)
[195] Artillery battery
[196] Engineers
[197] UDF Forces
[198] 1,500–3,000 personnel
[199] Mortars, RPGs, small arms
[200] T-72 presence confirmed
[201] Strong cross-border support networks
[203] 5. PLANS DRAWN UP BY STAFF – DEFENSIVE CONTINGENCY OPTIONS
[204] PLAN A – HOLD THE COAST / AVOID PROVOCATION
[205] Consolidate around:
[206] Port,
[207] Main junction,
[208] Fuel/ammo depots.
[209] Increase patrols & early warning.
[210] Advantages:
[211] Low political risk.
[212] Avoids triggering full Croatian offensive.
[213] Disadvantages:
[214] Yields initiative.
[215] Allows UDF infiltration.
[217] PLAN B – ELASTIC DEFENSE / ARMORED COUNTER-ATTACK
[218] Use 3rd Infantry to hold fixed points.
[219] Deploy 2nd Armored Angels for:
[220] Rapid counterattack against Croatian spearheads,
[221] Encirclement of isolated UDF groups.
[222] Advantages:
[223] Retains mobility.
[224] Uses armored assets before Croatian artillery suppresses them.
[225] Disadvantages:
[226] High fuel cost.
[227] Abrams reliability low.
[228] If counterattack fails, line collapses.
[230] PLAN C – PREEMPTIVE SHAPING OPERATIONS
[231] Limited airstrikes (if justified) on UDF armor & staging areas.
[232] Recon raids into suspected Croatian forward observation posts.
[233] Sabotage teams targeting Croatian bridgeheads.
[234] Advantages:
[235] Disrupts enemy build-up.
[236] Sends political signal.
[237] Disadvantages:
[238] Risk of escalation before we’re ready.
[239] Could justify Croatian offensive.
[241] PLAN D – STRATEGIC WITHDRAWAL TO HARDPOINTS
[242] Abandon inland outposts.
[243] Compress forces around:
[244] Port,
[245] Coastal fortifications,
[246] Preset defensive zones.
[247] Advantages:
[248] Dense defense, easier supply.
[249] Reduces UDF ambush exposure.
[250] Disadvantages:
[251] Cedes territory.
[252] Encourages Croatian claim of “Reunion retreat.”
[254] 6. CLOSE CALLS (PAST 72 HOURS)
[255] Artillery shells landed within 200m of our Site D-12 ammo dump.
[256] Likely deliberate ranging.
[257] If they walk fire in 2–3km, the dump is lost.
[258] UDF ambush on convoy near inland road P-7.
[259] No casualties, but AT gun emplacement was pre-dug.
[260] SIGINT detected Croatian artillery nets referencing “Blue Eagle axis,” believed to be our primary reinforcement corridor.
[261] Croatian recon patrol crossed 300m into our territory before retreating when spotted.
[262] Testing reaction time.
[264] 7. CROATIAN PRESIDENT (FOR RECORD)
[265] President Franjo Tuđman
[266] Nationalist, strategic opportunist.
[267] Sees Dalmatia as Croatian by right and Reunion as temporary occupier.
[268] Believes Reunion is overextended after Evinos.
[269] His military council is pushing for a late ’92 or early ’93 correction operation.
[271] 8. RNIO CONCLUSION (BLUNT)
[272] Croatia is preparing the battlefield.
[273] UDF is no longer a guerrilla sideshow; it is becoming a forward element of Croatian operational planning.
[274] Your helicopter being shot down marks the transition from covert hostility to deliberate pressure.
[275] If we do nothing, Croatia will:
[276] Finish massing forces,
[277] Let UDF soften our logistics,
[278] Launch a limited offensive that forces a political settlement unfavorable to us.
[279] Dalmatia will slip away.
[280] Unless we reshape the situation NOW.

[1] REUNION OIL
[3] 1) What Parliament “goes for” (the law that passes)
[4] BILL No. 201/1992 — Offshore Petroleum Sovereignty & Strategic Development Act (OPSSDA)
[5] Passed: 6 October 1992
 Sponsors: RRP (institutionalists) + RCA (industrial royalists) + NSF (security caucus) with negotiated LUP add-ons
 Committees: Energy & Industry; Finance; National Security; Public Procurement (oversight insertions)
[6] Core deal inside the bill
[7] 80% Nationalized / 20% Privatized by production entitlement (not land ownership).
[8] The state keeps a permanent 80% participating interest through a new NOC holding vehicle.
[9] Private firms compete for slices of the 20% production share via tenders.
[10] Export control: private production can only be sold to approved markets/buyers set by Cabinet (and can be restricted in crisis).
[11] Domestic supply obligation: a fixed minimum share must be offered to Reunion first at indexed prices (to prevent domestic energy blackmail).
[12] Signature bonus + FX terms: every winning consortium pays an upfront signature bonus (in USD/ECU or equivalent hard currency) into a ring-fenced Stabilization Account.
[13] Security vetting: all foreign technical staff on critical assets get Interior/RNIA vetting.
[14] Fast-track permitting: timelines are compressed, but “minimum safety” language stays (LUP forced that in).
[15] Greece clause (quiet but crucial): development in the shared basin is contingent on a unitization / joint development understanding for the portion that lies between Reunion and Greece / in Greek waters.
[16] Committee fingerprints
[17] RRP: forced competitive tender rules + public registry of contract awards.
[18] RCA: carved out a “National Champion Preference” scoring category (this is how Royla doesn’t get boxed out).
[19] NSF: security veto power on foreign staff and remote diagnostics systems.
[20] LUP: forced a domestic supply obligation + worker training requirements + a modest environmental floor.
[21] Vote (400 seats)
[22] RRP: 106 For / 8 Against / 4 Abstain
[23] RCA: 74 For / 8 Against / 0 Abstain
[24] LUP: 61 For / 28 Against / 6 Abstain
[25] NSF: 56 For / 4 Against / 2 Abstain
[26] Dalmatian lists/minors: 23 For / 14 Against / 2 Abstain
 Total: 320 For / 62 Against / 14 Abstain (4 absent)
[27] Why it passes: everyone wants the story that “Reunion has a solvent future,” even if they’re terrified of who gets rich.
[29] 2) Who bids, what they ask for, and how the pie gets split
[30] How the tender is structured
[31] Finance + Energy split the privatized 20% into four “production entitlement tranches,” because it prevents one foreign major from owning the political narrative:
[32] Tranche A: 6%
[33] Tranche B: 6%
[34] Tranche C: 4%
[35] Tranche D: 4%
 (Total: 20%)
[36] Each tranche includes:
[37] capital commitments (survey → appraisal → early production),
[38] local content requirements,
[39] training programs,
[40] and an offtake plan consistent with Reunion’s “approved buyers” policy.
[41] Major external bidders (lobbying starts immediately)
[42] Shell (aggressive: wants operatorship, promises fast offshore execution)
[43] Exxon (aggressive: wants operatorship, offers hard-currency bonus + technical depth)
[44] BP (bids but is politically vulnerable—Croatia optics makes Parliament skittish)
[45] Total and/or Elf Aquitaine (France plays the “friendly strategic partner” angle hard)
[46] ENI/Agip (bids as a Mediterranean specialist; offers refinery/adaptation packages)
[47] Domestic bidders / consortia
[48] Younger Industries (major play: forms “Younger Offshore Consortium” and bids for a lead role)
[49] Royla (King Zo’s new oil company) huge capital backing, but brand-new and politically radioactive
[50] Other Reunion capital pools (banks/industrial groups) form “Reunion Coastal Energy” type vehicles to try to capture service contracts and minority stakes
[51] The award (what Finance/Parliament will accept in early October)
[52] Parliament’s center (RRP) insists on a split that:
[53] brings hard currency in immediately,
[54] secures real operators, and
[55] avoids giving one royal-linked firm too much control too fast.
[56] So the winning allocation typically looks like this:
[57] Final allocation of the privatized 20% (announced 10–12 October window)
[58] Tranche A — 6%: Exxon-led consortium (operator)
[59] Sells the bonus as: fastest appraisal, best offshore track record, biggest hard-currency signature bonus.
[60] Tranche B — 6%: Shell-led consortium (operator)
[61] Wins on: execution timeline + logistics plan + “EU market offtake readiness.”
[62] Tranche C — 4%: French-led consortium (Total/Elf) (or ENI if you want Italy stronger)
[63] Wins on: political trust + training + downstream/refining integration.
[64] Tranche D — 4%: Domestic “National Partner” tranche led by Younger Industries with Royla as a minority partner
[65] Younger gets the steering role because it has industry footprint and credibility.
[66] Royla gets a foothold (and prestige), but not enough to look like a royal seizure of the sector.
[67] In practice, each foreign-led tranche is required to carry a Reunion partner stake (often 10–25% inside the consortium), but the production entitlement split above is what the public and Parliament fixate on.
[69] 3) The political side-effects (immediate, in early October)
[70] Younger Industries
[71] Treated as “patriotic industrial capital.”
[72] RRP likes it because it looks like modernization; RCA likes it because it looks nationalist; LUP mistrusts it but prefers it to pure foreign capture.
[73] Royla (King Zo’s company)
[74] RCA and NSF quietly push it hard.
[75] RRP forces the “domestic tranche only + minority” compromise to avoid a public meltdown over monarchy profiteering during war.
[76] Curro “small play”
[77] This instantly becomes an ethics scandal magnet even if the investment is indirect. Expect:
[78] Justice Ministry to demand disclosure frameworks (“blind trust or divest” logic),
[79] a Parliamentary Ethics Subcommittee emergency hearing,
[80] and the RBD/press framing it as: “Is Finance minister personally exposed to decisions he’s regulating?”
[81] Even if Curro did nothing illegal, optics are brutal.
[83] 4) What Parliament demands next (the conditions they attach)
[84] If you want this to feel real, Parliament will attach “must-do” conditions within days:
[85] A Petroleum Stabilization Fund (even if small at first) so oil doesn’t become instant corruption.
[86] Hard-currency ringfencing for imports/debt service (to calm markets).
[87] A Greek unitization track (quiet diplomacy) — because investors will not fund a cross-border legal war.
[88] Local content quotas (jobs, training, domestic service firms).
[89] Export approval regime explicitly favoring “European markets” without legally locking you into a club you aren’t in yet.
[92] At 1.2M bpd, your annual volume is:
[93] 1.2M × 365 = 438,000,000 barrels/year (438M bbl/yr)
[94] If you could magically “switch” the stream from heavy to light (i.e., it sells like a light sweet crude instead of taking a heavy discount), the revenue jump is basically:
 (heavy discount removed) × 438M barrels, then apply your state take.
[95] Key assumption (the only thing that really matters)
[96] Heavy crude typically sells at a discount to benchmark light crude. A reasonable planning range is:
[97] Heavy discount vs light: $8–$15 per barrel (sometimes more, but this is a solid “planning band”)
[99] 1) Government revenue at 1.2M bpd if sold as “light”
[100] Earlier, for heavy at 1.2M bpd, I gave a government take of ~$4.27B/yr (based on a mid state-take and heavy netback).
[101] If the oil sells as light, your government take increases by roughly:
[102] Extra gov $/bbl = discount removed × state take
[103] Use 55–65% as a normal state take band
[104] Extra government revenue from switching heavy → light
[105] Low case: $8 × 55% = $4.40/bbl → 438M × 4.40 = $1.93B/yr
[106] High case: $15 × 65% = $9.75/bbl → 438M × 9.75 = $4.27B/yr
[107] New government revenue (light equivalent)
[108] Add that to the heavy-case $4.27B/yr:
[109] Low case: $4.27B + $1.93B = $6.20B/yr
[110] High case: $4.27B + $4.27B = $8.54B/yr
[111] Convert to RMC at $1 = 5.8 RMC:
[112] $6.20B → 35.96B RMC/yr
[113] $8.54B → 49.53B RMC/yr
[114] So: light-equivalent at 1.2M bpd = roughly $6.2B–$8.5B per year to the state, or ~36B–50B RMC/yr.
[116] 2) Gross sales revenue (total oil sales) at 1.2M bpd
[117] If you want total sales before costs/state take, it’s:
[118] Gross = 438M bbl × realized price
[119] Example quick anchors:
[120] At $20/bbl: $8.76B/yr (50.8B RMC)
[121] At $30/bbl: $13.14B/yr (76.2B RMC)
