sources.text:
[1] 1946 CONSTITUTION – OUTLINE
[2] 1. Preamble & Foundational Principles
[3] Adopted after the 1930s civil war and the collapse of the old absolute monarchy.
[4] Core ideas:
[5] Reunion is a democratic republic built to prevent:
[6] One-party rule,
[7] Military dictatorship,
[8] Absolute monarchy returning.
[9] It acknowledges:
[10] The “historic role of the Crown” and keeps the King as a symbolic Head of State,
[11] But vests real power in elected institutions.
[12] No one’s touched the text since 1946; all the bending has been done via ordinary laws and “interpretation.”
[14] 2. Article I – The State & Institutions
[15] Form of State
[16] “Unitary, indivisible Republic of Reunion.”
[17] Islands (Northern / Central / Southern / Dalmatia / fringe islands) recognized as administrative regions, not full federal units.
[18] The monarchy is described as a “hereditary Crown within the Republic, guardian of continuity and dignity of the State.”
[19] Separation of Powers
[20] Legislative: Assembly of the Republic (unicameral).
[21] Executive: President of the Republic + Council of Ministers.
[22] Judiciary: independent courts, plus a Constitutional Court.
[23] Outdated part:
 Text still references a “President of the Council of Ministers” as if there’s a Prime Minister, but in practice that role has fused into the Presidency by statute and custom. The constitution was never updated to reflect that.
[25] 3. Article II – Rights & Duties of Citizens
[26] This is your de-facto “bill of rights.” It’s noble and also shot through with 1940s paranoia.
[27] Citizenship
[28] Jus sanguinis as default:
[29] Child of a Reunionist citizen is a citizen.
[30] Jus soli only for:
[31] Children born on Reunion soil to stateless parents or unknown parentage.
[32] Naturalization:
[33] Left to statute (see Immigration Code below).
[34] Equality Clause
[35] “All citizens are equal before the law without distinction of origin, creed, or political conviction.”
[36] Then a nasty fudge line:
[37] “The law may provide distinctions where required to protect public order, public morals, or the national character.”
[38] That “national character” phrase is a legal cancer – it justifies all sorts of abuse.
[39] Fundamental Rights
[40] Textually guaranteed:
[41] Freedom of expression, press, and opinion.
[42] Freedom of assembly and association.
[43] Freedom of religion and conscience.
[44] Inviolability of the home and correspondence.
[45] Right to due process and defense in criminal matters.
[46] Right to vote and stand for office at age 18.
[47] But all of them are subject to a familiar carve-out:
 “except as limited by law in the interests of security, public order, and the protection of the democratic and republican order.”
[48] That’s the hole every government has driven a truck through.
[49] Duties
[50] Pay taxes.
[51] Serve in the defense of the Republic (basis for conscription law).
[52] Respect the Constitution and “democratic institutions.”
[54] 4. Article III – Executive Power
[55] President of the Republic
[56] Election:
[57] Direct popular vote.
[58] Term: 4 years.
[59] Re-election:
[60] No limit to terms
[61] Non-consecutive terms allowed (hence multiple Hartmann-party presidents across decades).
[62] Powers:
[63] Appoints and dismisses ministers and the “President of the Council” (Prime Minister in theory, merged into President in practice).
[64] Promulgates laws; can send a bill back once for reconsideration.
[65] Can call referendums on major constitutional/political issues.
[66] Supreme Commander of Armed Forces.
[67] Can declare a State of Emergency (see Article IV).
[68] May dissolve the Assembly once per term lasting a duration of 3 months with additional extensions granted of up to 6 month extensions at a time. new elections will be held for parliament.
[69] The constitution never codified the current “no Prime Minister” reality. Legally, a hostile Assembly could try to argue parts of the executive architecture are unconstitutional.
[70] The King
[71] Symbolic Head of State:
[72] Signs treaties ceremonially.
[73] Delivers annual “Address to the Nation.”
[74] Has the right to be consulted, to counsel, and to warn.
[75] Reserve powers (vaguely drafted):
[76] In “grave constitutional crisis,” the King may:
[77] Appeal directly to the people,
[78] Request the Assembly to reconsider legislation that, in his view, “gravely harms the constitutional order”.
[79] All of this requires countersignature from the President or a Minister to be valid, but the text is hazy enough that royalists and republicans can both spin it.
[81] 5. Article IV – Legislature
[82] Assembly of the Republic
[83] Originally 200 members, elected every 4 years.
[84] Constitution text: “The Assembly shall consist of no fewer than 150 and no more than 300 deputies.”
[85] You recently expanded to 400 seats by statute – strictly speaking, that’s constitutionally dubious. Halvik knows it; everyone decided not to open that can of worms… yet.
[86] Electoral system:
[87] Proportional representation, multi-member constituencies by island/region.
[88] Parties must respect “democratic principles”; openly anti-democratic parties may be banned by law.
[89] Powers:
[90] Passes ordinary laws, budget, taxes.
[91] Can impeach the President (2/3 majority) for “high crimes and grave violations of the Constitution.”
[92] Confirms key appointments (Constitutional Court, some judges, RNIA Director under new statute).
[94] 6. Article V – Judiciary
[95] Guarantees judicial independence “subject only to the Constitution and the law.”
[96] Constitutional Court
[97] 9 judges.
[98] Appointed by:
[99] President (3),
[100] Assembly (3),
[101] King (3).
[102] 12-year non-renewable terms.
[103] Powers:
[104] Review laws for constitutionality.
[105] Rule on disputes between state organs.
[106] Rule on party bans and some electoral disputes.
[107] In practice, appointments have been heavily politicized; this Court has been more cautious than assertive.
[108] Ordinary Courts
[109] Supreme Court of Cassation at the top.
[110] Regional courts and local courts under it.
[112] 7. Article VI – Emergency & Security Provisions
[113] President can declare a State of Emergency:
[114] Initially for up to 90 days.
[115] Must be notified to Assembly within 24 hours.
[116] Assembly can approve, modify, or revoke by simple majority.
[117] Under emergency:
[118] Freedom of assembly and strike may be suspended.
[119] Curfews imposed.
[120] Extended detention without charge up to 30 days.
[121] Military and RIA can be deployed internally under special rules.
[122] This is the legal basis for the communist crackdowns, the martial law in Reunion City after the Parliament attack, etc.
[123] No modern safeguards – no explicit prohibition on torture, no explicit ban on blanket censorship.
[125] 8. Article VII – Amendments
[126] Amendments require:
[127] 2/3 majority in the Assembly.
[128] A second 2/3 vote at least six months later.
[129] Countersignature by President and King.
[130] Optional referendum if 1/3 of Assembly or President requests it.
[131] Threshold is so high that everyone has preferred to work around the constitution instead of updating it. That’s why it’s still half-1946, half-ad hoc practice.
[133] II. KEY LAWS – OUTLINE
[134] Now, the main legal pillars sitting on top of that constitution, shaped by your presidential list:
[135] 1. Electoral & Parties Law
[136] Electoral Law of 1952, revised 1968, 1981:
[137] Establishes PR system, seat allocation, thresholds.
[138] Parties must register and accept constitutional order.
[139] Party bans allowed for:
[140] Advocating violent overthrow,
[141] Explicitly anti-democratic ideologies.
[142] Parties & Campaign Finance Act (1981):
[143] Regulates donations, public funding.
[144] Very weak enforcement until recently; lots of loopholes oligarchs and factions exploit.
[146] 2. Immigration & Nationality Framework
[147] Primarily:
[148] Immigration & Nationality Code of 1971
[149] Amended 1983 (post-Hartmann leftist era) and 1990 (in response to Greek and Balkan instability).
[150] Key points:
[151] Entry & Residence:
[152] Visa regime with:
[153] Preference for:
[154] Reunion diaspora,
[155] Skilled workers,
[156] Investors.
[157] Broad discretion to deny entry for:
[158] “Threats to the constitutional order,”
[159] National security,
[160] Serious criminal record.
[161] This has historically been used to keep out both foreign communists and foreign right-wing militants.
[162] Naturalization:
[163] Standard path:
[164] 10 years legal residence.
[165] Language and civic test.
[166] Clean criminal record.
[167] Demonstrated “integration into Reunion society.”
[168] Diaspora / ethnic-return path:
[169] 3–5 years residence, test may be waived.
[170] Designed to bring back Reunionists or their descendants.
[171] Asylum / Refugees:
[172] 1990 Asylum Law brought in:
[173] Narrow asylum grounds.
[174] Very high bar for proof.
[175] Broad discretion for Interior and Security to deny on “security” grounds.
[176] This is all very 20th-century – restrictive, opaque, and ripe for abuse. It also has basically no modern framework for long-term migrant integration.
[178] 3. Freedom of Expression, Press & Public Order
[179] Grounded in several acts:
[180] Public Order & Social Peace Act (1950)
[181] Bans “organizations advocating the violent overthrow of the constitutional order.”
[182] Allows authorities to ban demonstrations if they “threaten public peace or constitutional values.”
[183] Press & Broadcast Act (1962)
[184] Licensing for broadcast media.
[185] Defamation criminalized.
[186] “Insulting the Crown or the Republic’s institutions” is a criminal offence.
[187] Vague “offence to public morals” clause allows censorship.
[188] National Security & Subversive Activities Act (1977) (Hartmann-era, leftist security obsessions):
[189] Criminalizes:
[190] “Propaganda in service of a foreign power hostile to the Republic.”
[191] “Apology for political violence.”
[192] Used primarily against communists in Torrental protests, but on paper it’s ideology-agnostic.
[193] De jure, free speech exists. De facto:
[194] The state has wide latitude to ban gatherings and speech that it deems:
[195] “Subversive,”
[196] “Anti-constitutional,” or
[197] “Morally harmful.”
[198] Halvik, if he wants a freer modern state, has to either:
[199] Reform these laws, or
[200] Push constitutional court challenges against their vaguer parts.
[202] 4. Term Limits & Presidency in Law
[203] Beyond the Constitution:
[204] Presidential Elections Act (1951)
[205] Clarifies:
[206] 4-year term.
[207] Two consecutive terms maximum per individual.
[208] Non-consecutive terms allowed.
[209] Provides:
[210] If the President dies or resigns:
[211] The Speaker of the Assembly becomes Acting President until elections in 90 days.
[212] There’s no statutory recall mechanism; only impeachment (2/3 Assembly) and elections. That’s why Strevo stepping down after his stroke requires a political, not legal, process.
[214] 5. Defense, RIA/RNIA & Internal Security
[215] Defense & Armed Forces Act (1963)
[216] Codifies civilian control; conscription; structure of army, navy, air force.
[217] RIA Statute (1969)
[218] Created RIA as hybrid internal security + intelligence organ.
[219] Granted broad powers under emergency conditions:
[220] Surveillance,
[221] Detention handoff,
[222] Internal ops.
[223] RNIA Reorganization Act (1992)
[224] Your new law:
[225] Creates RNIA as a separate, civilian intel agency.
[226] Strips RIA of formal intel analysis role; redefines it as a national-guard-like security force.
[227] Adds parliamentary oversight and a 3/5 confirmation rule for RNIA Director.
[228] The Constitution hasn’t been updated to reflect this dual structure; it still speaks vaguely of “security organs.”
[230] 6. Criminal Code & Procedure
[231] Still largely based on:
[232] Penal Code 1948, heavily amended but structurally old.
[233] Code of Criminal Procedure 1954.
[234] Problems:
[235] Outdated offences remain:
[236] “Insult to foreign heads of state.”
[237] Broad “offence to public morals.”
[238] “Subversive assembly” with vague wording.
[239] Procedural issues:
[240] Pre-trial detention rules were written with internal wars and political violence in mind; authorities can hold suspects longer than most modern European systems.
[241] Weak protection of the right to counsel during the first 24–48 hours of detention, especially under emergency laws.
[242] If Halvik wants to modernize justice, this is a prime target.
[244] 7. Labor, Unions & Strikes
[245] Labor Relations Act (1960) and Trade Union Act (1974):
[246] Recognize unions and the right to strike.
[247] But:
[248] Strikes can be banned in a wide range of “essential services.”
[249] Emergency laws let the state suspend strikes at will.

[1] I. NUCLEAR + INFRASTRUCTURE: JOBS & MACRO IMPACT
[2] Assumptions (using the scale we’ve been playing with):
[3] GDP: ~18–20 billion RMC equivalent
[4] Your signed Infrastructure + Clean Power package over the first term (4–5 years) is realistically in the 1.5–2.0 billion RMC total capital range if you don’t want a fiscal heart attack.
[5] 1. Jobs from Infrastructure + Nuclear (First Term)
[6] Rule-of-thumb multipliers (Reunion conditions, not fantasy):
[7] For infrastructure construction (roads, rail, ports, grid):
[8] Each 100 million RMC in capital spend supports roughly:
[9] 1,500–2,000 direct construction/engineering job-years
[10] 2,000–3,000 indirect/induced job-years (cement, steel, services, shops, etc.)
[11] For nuclear plant refit (heavily specialized and tech-heavy):
[12] Each 100 million RMC supports about:
[13] 1,000–1,200 direct job-years (engineers, welders, safety techs, etc.)
[14] 1,500–2,000 indirect job-years
[15] So if your combined program over 4–5 years looks like:
[16] ~1.2–1.4 billion RMC in infrastructure
[17] ~500–700 million RMC in Lucania plant refit
[18] You’re looking at, over a full term:
[19] Total direct job-years:
[20] Infrastructure: ~18,000–28,000
[21] Nuclear refit: ~5,000–8,000
[22] Combined: ~23,000–36,000 direct job-years
[23] Total indirect/induced job-years:
[24] Infrastructure: ~24,000–40,000
[25] Nuclear refit: ~7,500–14,000
[26] Combined: ~31,500–54,000 indirect job-years
[27] Spread over 4–5 years, that’s on the order of:
[28] 10,000–15,000 jobs per year (direct + indirect) in the real economy, not counting the long-term permanent jobs that remain afterward.
[29] 2. Long-Term Growth Impact
[30] If you keep it tight and don’t let corruption eat half of it:
[31] Baseline post-war growth without big reforms: ~1–1.5% real GDP per year
[32] With disciplined infrastructure + nuclear refit:
[33] You can realistically push that to ~2–2.5% per year on average over a decade.
[34] In good years with exports behaving, you might touch 3%.
[35] Bottom line: if you don’t screw this up, these programs can roughly double the underlying growth rate compared to the stagnation scenario.
[37] II. INFRASTRUCTURE BILL – FIRST TERM ACHIEVEMENTS BY REGION
[38] Roughly prioritizing as you implied: Central first, then North/Lucania, Dalmatia and fringe following.
[39] 1. Central Island (Reunion City + hinterland)
[40] Timeline: Years 1–3 are where most visible progress happens here.
[41] What you can realistically complete by end of first term:
[42] Major port upgrade in Reunion City:
[43] New cranes, IT/logistics system, partial berth reinforcement.
[44] Cuts turnaround times and reduces ship logjams.
[45] Key arterial roads:
[46] Main industrial belt ring-road resurfaced and widened.
[47] A couple of major bottleneck bridges upgraded.
[48] Grid stabilization in industrial zones:
[49] New substations and upgraded transformers feeding factories and dockside.
[50] Impact:
[51] Immediate bump in export capacity and efficiency.
[52] Reduced shipping delays and industrial downtime.
[53] Central Island becomes the “proof of concept” you can point to: “Look what competent spending does.”
[55] 2. Northern Island & Lucania
[56] Timeline: Years 2–5, with Lucania’s nuclear plant refit overlapping.
[57] Infrastructure:
[58] Rural spine roads:
[59] One north-south corridor across the island, plus a set of lateral roads connecting farming/mining regions to that spine.
[60] Rail modernization (partial):
[61] One key corridor linking Lucanian interior/extractives to main ports and industrial nodes.
[62] Don’t fantasize about full network renewal in one term; you pick the most commercially important line and fix that.
[63] Impact:
[64] Lower transport costs for crops and minerals.
[65] Rural regions feel the state’s presence for the first time in decades, which matters politically.
[67] 3. Dalmatia
[68] Timeline: Mostly Years 3–5, partly constrained by security.
[69] Infrastructure you can plausibly move on:
[70] Port repairs/upgrades in one major Dalmatian city:
[71] Focus on dual-use: civilian shipping + naval logistics.
[72] Selective road upgrades:
[73] Connect Dalmatian coastal corridor to inland towns you want firmly in the Reunion orbit (not the ones you’re unsure you can hold politically).
[74] Impact:
[75] Anchors your “we’re rebuilding you, not occupying you” message.
[76] Makes Dalmatian exports and tourism less of a sick joke.
[78] 4. Fringe Islands
[79] Timeline: Years 3–6+, most likely spill into the next term.
[80] Realistic first-term goals:
[81] One or two flagship projects:
[82] A small port upgrade and power reliability project on a key fringe island.
[83] Symbolic but real:
[84] Shows the fringe you haven't forgotten them, and capitalizes on your own history working those islands.
[86] III. NUCLEAR: REUNION PLANT PAUSE VS LUCANIA TRIDENT REFIT
[87] You’re absolutely right to be cautious about pushing a brand-new plant in the capital after the Trident scandal. People remember “almost melted down in ’68,” even if they weren’t born.
[88] 1. Pausing the New Reunion City Plant
[89] What this does:
[90] Benefits:
[91] Avoids massive up-front costs and political backlash around siting, safety, and “Chernobyl in the capital” fear.
[92] Frees capacity (political and financial) to focus on Lucania refit and grid modernization first.
[93] Costs:
[94] Delays the long-term dream of making the capital the showpiece of ultra-cheap nuclear power.
[95] Some contractors and foreign partners will sulk; they wanted big ticket contracts in the capital.
[96] You keep the land and designs in reserve as Phase 2 if Lucania refit goes well.
[98] 2. Lucania Trident Plant Refit – Numbers
[99] Capital Cost (Very Rough Ballpark)
[100] Refit and safety modernization of an old plant is expensive but cheaper than a full new build.
[101] Estimate:
[102] 600–800 million RMC over 5–7 years.
[103] Includes:
[104] Full safety system overhaul (cooling, containment, control systems).
[105] Structural reinforcement of key buildings.
[106] New control room and digital instrumentation.
[107] Environmental remediation and monitoring systems.
[108] Training and recruitment of a modern, safety-first workforce.
[109] Jobs
[110] Using the multipliers above and accounting for specialized nature:
[111] Construction/refit period (5–7 years):
[112] 1,200–1,500 direct jobs at peak,
[113] 2,000–2,500 indirect jobs (suppliers, services, local economy).
[114] Permanent operating jobs once online:
[115] ~400–600 high-quality permanent jobs:
[116] Engineers, operators, safety staff, security, maintenance.
[117] Plus additional grid and support jobs downstream.
[118] Timeline (If You Actually Push It)
[119] Year 0–1:
[120] Detailed safety and structural assessment, regulatory framework update.
[121] Political fights, but if managed, you end Year 1 with a signed master plan.
[122] Years 1–3:
[123] Major civil and systems work.
[124] Employment at peak.
[125] Progressive safety reviews.
[126] Years 3–4:
[127] Systems integration, fuel loading prep, initial low-power testing.
[128] Year 4–5:
[129] Full power startup, gradual ramp-up to nominal output.
[130] If you drag your feet with committees and infighting, add 1–2 years easily. If you run it like your life depends on it, first power in ~4–5 years is believable.
[131] Effect on Energy Prices & Security
[132] Once at full power, that plant could cover a significant chunk of national baseload (depending on the reactor size you decide in canon, but think a big bite).
[133] Expected impact:
[134] Wholesale electricity price:
[135] Can be pushed down by 10–20% over a decade, compared to a “fossil-heavy, underinvested grid” scenario.
[136] Price volatility:
[137] Decreases, because you’re less dependent on imported fuel price swings.
[138] Grid reliability in the north & Lucania:
[139] Jumps significantly.
[140] Fewer brownouts, more predictable power for industry and households.
[141] Politically, if you sell it right:
[142] “We took the country’s biggest nuclear embarrassment and turned it into a symbol of competence and discipline.”
[143] That’s powerful.
[145] IV. POTENTIAL CONTRACTORS – WHO ACTUALLY DOES THIS WORK
[146] You’re not going to let random cousins with a van build this.
[147] 1. Nuclear Refit – Likely Players
[148] Younger Industries
[149] Already proved they can do serious heavy engineering (nuclear submarine).
[150] Can lead or co-lead the refit consortium, especially on structural and systems engineering.
[151] Reunion Civil Engineering Group (RCEG)
[152] State-aligned major civil engineering firm.
[153] Handles concrete, structural reinforcement, auxiliary buildings.
[154] Foreign Nuclear Tech Partner
[155] You’ll need a Western or allied partner:
[156] For safety systems, controls, and regulatory best practices.
[157] This is where France or another European player can plug in.
[158] You structure it as a joint venture with clear contractual performance and safety requirements.
[160] 2. Infrastructure – Likely Players
[161] Reunion Rail & Transit Consortium (RRTC)
[162] For rail modernization projects.
[163] Lucania & Northern Roads Cooperative Groups
[164] Mid-sized firms that can handle rural road and bridge works if properly overseen.
[165] Dalmatian Ports & Shipyards Group
[166] For Dalmatian port repair and joint civilian/naval dock facilities.
[167] You deliberately avoid giving everything to one mega-contractor; spread it enough to avoid monopoly, but not so wide that oversight becomes impossible.
[169] V. TIMING BY REGION – WHEN DO PEOPLE ACTUALLY SEE RESULTS?
[170] You wanted a sense of who feels it first, so you can plan messaging and growth.
[171] Year 1–2
[172] Visible work in Reunion City:
[173] Port cranes, roadworks, substations.
[174] Lucania:
[175] Surveys and early works at Trident site.
[176] Jobs and money flow primarily to:
[177] Central Island urban workers,
[178] Higher-skilled engineers and planners.
[179] Year 2–3
[180] Central Island:
[181] Major projects near completion, visible wins.
[182] Northern Island / Lucania:
[183] Road and rail works visibly ramping.
[184] Nuclear refit site employing hundreds.
[185] Year 3–5
[186] Lucania and Northern Island hit their stride:
[187] Roads, rail corridors, and the plant approaching startup.
[188] Dalmatia:
[189] Port works and some strategic roads show up.
[190] Fringe islands:
[191] One or two flagship projects.
[192] Rough emotional map:
[193] Central Island feels it first and most consistently.
[194] Lucania/North feel it second but get the bigger long-term gain thanks to the plant + agricultural logistics.
[195] Dalmatia and fringe feel it later but symbolically critical.
[197] VI. FULL AUDIT – “FOR THE PRESIDENT’S EYES ONLY”
[198] This is where Emilio sharpens the knife.
[199] A serious audit of government expenditure will almost certainly find:
[200] 1. Redundant / Obsolete Security Programs
[201] Wartime emergency funds still bleeding out for:
[202] “Temporary” security detachments,
[203] Intelligence projects that no longer exist,
[204] Special operations slush lines.
[205] Estimated potential savings:
[206] 1–2% of total budget over 2–3 years if you are ruthless and backed politically.
[207] 2. Zombie State-Owned Enterprises & Subsidies
[208] SOEs in:
[209] Heavy industry, outdated factories, and old shipping/fleet companies that:
[210] Lose money yearly,
[211] Provide little strategic value now that war is over.
[212] Potential savings / reallocation:
[213] 1–1.5% of budget, if:
[214] You freeze hiring,
[215] Cut loss-making offsets,
[216] Force restructuring or partial privatization.
[217] 3. Prestige / Vanity Spending
[218] Overfunded:
[219] Ceremonial budgets,
[220] Ministries duplicating each other’s cultural and “development” projects,
[221] Overseas “friendship missions” that do nothing.
[222] Potential savings:
[223] 0.5–1% of budget, politically sensitive but doable if framed as “we tighten our belts together”.
[224] 4. Inefficient Tax Expenditures
[225] Tax breaks and exemptions:
[226] For sectors that no longer need them,
[227] For old political allies,
[228] For loopholes exploited by big business.
[229] Reforming these doesn’t cut spending directly, but raises revenue:
[230] Worth 1–2% of GDP over a few years if done carefully.

[1] MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT
[2] SUBJECT: Operational Necessity and State Survival — T-Minus 9.5 Hours
[3] CLASSIFICATION: TOP SECRET / EYES ONLY
[4] DATE: 02 OCTOBER 1992 | 10:30 HOURS
[5] I. THE PLOČE CONUNDRUM: THE TACTICAL SURRENDER
[6] The situation north of Ploče has moved beyond a local security incident. It is now the primary lever being used to dismantle your administration. The "Green Beret" insurgents holding the village have direct communication lines to the Bosnian factions holding the "Mastermind" dossier.
[7] Operational Recommendation:
[8] The state must facilitate the peaceful release and exit of the insurgents currently holding the village. This is a bitter pill, but it is the only path to achieving two critical objectives:
[9] Blackmail Suppression: The Bosnian entities have made it clear: if their men are "liquidated" or arrested, the full dossier naming you as the personal mastermind of the arms scheme will be released to every major news desk in the Mediterranean. Allowing their exit buys a temporary "silence window" to handle the Serbian threat.
[10] UN and International De-escalation: The UN observers at the screening point are looking for any excuse to flag a "Humanitarian Violation." A peaceful resolution satisfies the UN’s mandate, prevents a "Material Breach" declaration from Croatia, and ensures the first $30M US Tranche is not frozen on October 5th.
[11] The Brutal Reality: To the public and the NSF, this will look like a total capitulation. We must frame this as a "Humanitarian Gesture for the Hostages" to protect your Legitimacy (LG) from a total collapse.
[13] II. FISCAL AUDIT: THE 500 BILLION RMC HOLE
[14] Reunion’s GDP has stabilized at 2.4 Trillion RMC (~$414B USD), representing a staggering 17.2% drop from the 2.9T RMC baseline.
[15] Primary Causes of the Collapse:
[16] The Insurance Wall: Shipping through the Adriatic now carries a "War Risk" surcharge that has increased export costs for our rare earths by 350%.
[17] The Lockbox Credit Freeze: The Banking Bloc has frozen 40% of private credit lines. They fear that since the US has a lien on all port revenue, the state will default on its domestic obligations to pay the 12% US interest.
[18] The Horizon Dynamics "Stall": We have consolidated the defense industry, but we lack the high-tech electronics to finish the products. We are sitting on 115B RMC of "Dead Capital"—tanks and jets that are 90% complete but cannot fight.
[19] Economic Risk Matrix:
[20] Total Currency Devaluation (88% Risk): If the Street Rate hits 7.0:1 (currently 6.4:1), the RMC burns.
[21] Infrastructure Failure (50% Risk): If we cannot secure German engineers for Lucania, the A-1 Rail Spine will have no power by December.
[23] III. GEOPOLITICAL FLASHPOINTS & SOVIET POSTURE
[24] The "Somov Doctrine" is now in full effect. The Soviet Union is using the Mediterranean as a theater to project its new military-socialist strength.
[25] The Soviet Encirclement (Risk: 75%):
[26] Greece/Bulgaria: Intelligence confirms the 103rd Guards VDV and a tank brigade are establishing "Forward Security Zones" in People's Greece. This effectively places our Northern Island in a Soviet artillery vise.
[27] The Oil Threat: Our naval surveillance picked up "Ghost Contacts" near the offshore survey sites. If we drill without Soviet permission, they will likely declare a "Maritime Safety Zone" and seize the rigs.
[28] The Croatian "Material Breach" (Risk: 60%):
[29] Croatia is looking for any reason to void the 12-year peace. If we move a single National Guard unit into Dalmatia to handle the unrest caused by the Serbian leaks, Zagreb will declare a "Hostile Act" and launch a "Correction Operation" to retake everything down to the Šibenik line.
[31] IV. PUBLIC OPINION ENGINE (CURRENT STATUS)
[32] Metric
[33] Score
[34] Trend
[35] Status
[36] Security Confidence
[37] 44
[38] 📉
[39] Nationalists fear the Ploče surrender.
[40] Economic Hope
[41] 33
[42] 📉
[43] CRITICAL: Below the 35 threshold.
[44] Legitimacy
[45] 41
[46] 📉
[47] Serbian "Mastermind" leaks are working.
[48] Timeline of Imminent Events:
[49] T-Minus 9.5 Hours: Serbian Deadline. Failure to call Belgrade results in the "Dossier Dump" to the UN and LUP.
[50] October 5: $30M US Tranche deadline. Requires UN "Clean Resolution" of the Ploče crisis.
[51] October 15: Soviet Baltic Fleet arrival.
[52] Executive Decision Required:
[53] Do we authorize the peaceful exit of the Ploče insurgents to secure the Bosnian blackmail silence, or do we risk the "Dossier Dump" to maintain a "Strongman" image for the NSF?
[54] EYES ONLY: THE "REUNION FIRST" ACTION PLAN
[55] PREPARED BY: THE PRESIDENTIAL INNER CIRCLE (OFF-THE-RECORD) FOR: PRESIDENT DAX DONAHUE II SUBJECT: EXECUTION STRATEGY FOR THE SEPTEMBER CRISIS
[56] The situation is no longer a set of isolated problems; it is a synchronized assault on the Republic. To survive the next 72 hours, we must trade tactical "purity" for strategic survival.
[57] 1. The Ploče Exit (The Immediate Silence)
[58] The Move: Order the immediate, unconditional safe passage of the insurgents north of Ploče into Bosnia, facilitated by the UN.
[59] The Rationale: This satisfies the UN’s humanitarian mandate and secures the $30M US Tranche. More importantly, it honors the "Silence Agreement" with the Bosnian blackmailers.
[60] The Spin: Frame this as the "President’s Mercy." You are choosing the lives of the 80 hostages over the "vengeance" of a trial. It isolates the NSF hawks while looking statesperson-like to the West.
[61] 2. The Serbian Line (The 9-Hour Countdown)
[62] The Move: Call the Serbian President at 19:00—one hour before the deadline.
[63] The Offer: Do not admit guilt. Offer a "Joint Investigatory Commission" into the "unauthorized actions of junior financial officials."
[64] The Sacrifice: You must prepare a "Fall Guy." Curro is too vital for the A-1 Rail project to lose now, but a high-ranking Deputy in Finance must be "administratively isolated" by sunset to satisfy Belgrade’s demand for blood.
[65] 3. The RMC "Firewall" (Economic Defense)
[66] The Move: Release an emergency "Sovereign Oil Declaration."
[67] The Rationale: The market is panicking because they think the US owns the ports. We must announce that the 80% nationalized stake in the light-oil find is a "Permanent National Trust" that cannot be used for debt service.
[68] The Goal: Drive the Street Rate back below 6.0:1 by promising a future currency backed by oil, not just debt.
[69] 4. The Soviet Shadow (Deterrence)
[70] The Move: Order the Navy to a "Defensive Picket" at the mouth of Torrential Bay.
[71] The Rationale: Do not engage. If we go to the shared basin, we invite a Soviet "accident." By staying in our own territorial waters, we protect the mining exports (the actual money) while forcing the Soviets to be the ones who cross a red line if they want to provoke us.
[72] "Satellite imagery also confirms the arrival of four Tu-22M3 'Backfire' bombers at Tanagra. More disturbingly, ground observers report the presence of 'Special Handling Vans'—the type used by the Soviet 12th Main Directorate for tactical nuclear warhead transport. Somov isn't just blockading us; he's preparing a funeral pyre. If we fire on the Greek MiGs, we might be inviting a mushroom cloud over Reunion City."

[1] REPUBLIC OF REUNION
[2] REUNION NATIONAL INTELLIGENCE REORGANIZATION ACT, 1992
 (“RNIO Act 1992”)
[3] Passed by the Assembly on: [Date, e.g. 29 July 1992]
 Transmitted to the President on: [Date]
[5] SECTION 1 – SHORT TITLE AND PURPOSE
[6] This Act shall be cited as the Reunion National Intelligence Reorganization Act, 1992.
[7] The purposes of this Act are:
 a. To establish a unified, civilian Reunion National Intelligence Agency (RNIA) responsible for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of intelligence in defense of the Republic.
 b. To distinguish clearly between:
[8] Intelligence activities, and
[9] Domestic security and paramilitary functions.
 c. To reorganize the existing Reunion Intelligence Agency (RIA) and GRI so as to:
[10] Transfer intelligence functions to the RNIA, and
[11] Retain RIA as a separate National Guard–type domestic security and reserve force under law.
 d. To provide for democratic oversight, judicial safeguards, and accountability.
[13] SECTION 2 – DEFINITIONS
[14] For the purposes of this Act:
[15] “RNIA” means the Reunion National Intelligence Agency created under this Act.
[16] “RIA” means the Reunion Intelligence Agency in its reconstituted form as a national guard/security force as provided herein.
[17] “GRI” means the existing foreign and strategic intelligence body merged into the RNIA under this Act.
[18] “Intelligence activities” means the lawful collection, processing, analysis, and dissemination of information concerning:
[19] Foreign states,
[20] Non-state actors,
[21] Domestic threats to the constitutional order and national security,
 subject to this Act and applicable law.
[22] “Domestic operations” means any operations conducted within the territory of the Republic, including deployments of forces, patrols, arrests, or other coercive measures.
[24] SECTION 3 – ESTABLISHMENT OF THE RNIA
[25] There is hereby created a civilian agency to be known as the Reunion National Intelligence Agency (RNIA).
[26] The RNIA shall:
 a. Be responsible for strategic and operational intelligence concerning threats foreign and domestic;
 b. Operate under the constitutional authority of the President and the Assembly;
 c. Be prohibited from exercising arrest powers, conducting detentions, or engaging directly in kinetic operations, except in narrowly defined circumstances as provided by law and in cooperation with the appropriate security or police forces.
[27] The RNIA shall have the authority to:
 a. Collect intelligence by lawful means;
 b. Maintain liaison with foreign intelligence and security services with the authorization of the government;
 c. Provide threat assessments and intelligence briefings to:
[28] The President,
[29] The Council of Ministers,
[30] The Assembly’s designated oversight committee, and
[31] Other bodies as may be authorized by law.
[33] SECTION 4 – DIRECTOR OF THE RNIA
[34] The RNIA shall be headed by a Director, who shall:
 a. Be appointed by the President of the Republic;
 b. Be confirmed by a three-fifths majority of the Assembly;
 c. Serve a single term of seven (7) years, removable only for:
[35] Proven misconduct,
[36] Incapacity, or
[37] Grave violation of law, on a two-thirds vote of the Assembly.
[38] No person may be appointed Director who:
 a. Within the last five (5) years has held the position of Director of RIA or GRI;
 b. Is currently serving as a member of the Assembly or in any party leadership position;
 c. Holds any other office of profit or command in the armed forces.
[39] The Director shall:
 a. Be a non-partisan civil servant;
 b. Be bound to provide full and truthful information to the Assembly’s oversight committee and, where appropriate, to the courts.
[40] (This is the clause that enrages NSF quietly; it blocks their old RIA chief.)
[42] SECTION 5 – TRANSFER OF INTELLIGENCE FUNCTIONS
[43] All intelligence analysis, strategic assessment, and foreign intelligence collection functions of the RIA are hereby transferred to the RNIA.
[44] All functions, records, archives, and assets of the GRI are hereby:
 a. Dissolved as a separate entity, and
 b. Transferred to the RNIA, which shall assume all lawful rights and responsibilities of the GRI relevant to intelligence activities.
[45] Personnel:
 a. Intelligence-analysis, foreign-intel, and technical-collection personnel of RIA and GRI may be transferred to the RNIA under:
[46] Merit-based selection, and
[47] Security vetting consistent with this Act.
 b. Personnel primarily engaged in paramilitary or domestic operational roles shall not be transferred as intelligence officers, except following:
[48] Retraining, and
[49] Reassignment under RNIA’s civilian employment standards.
[51] SECTION 6 – RECONSTITUTION OF THE RIA AS NATIONAL GUARD FORCE
[52] The RIA is hereby reconstituted as a National Guard–type domestic security force, distinct from the RNIA.
[53] The reconstituted RIA shall:
 a. Operate under a dedicated ministry or under the Ministry of Defense as determined by subsequent legislation;
 b. Consist of:
[54] Units trained and equipped for domestic security operations, civil defense, and support to police and armed forces in times of emergency;
[55] Personnel recruited and trained specifically for domestic operations, not as general reserves.
 c. Be prohibited from:
[56] Conducting independent intelligence operations, except tactical information gathering inherent in security deployments;
[57] Maintaining its own strategic intelligence-analysis directorates separate from RNIA.
[58] Rules of engagement, jurisdiction, and accountability of the reconstituted RIA shall be further specified by secondary legislation consistent with:
[59] The Constitution,
[60] This Act, and
[61] Acts concerning police and armed forces.
[63] SECTION 7 – OVERSIGHT AND SAFEGUARDS
[64] A permanent Assembly Committee on Intelligence and Security Oversight (“the Committee”) is hereby established to:
 a. Receive regular reports from the Director of RNIA;
 b. Review the legality, proportionality, and necessity of RNIA’s activities;
 c. Conduct inquiries into alleged abuses or violations by RNIA officers.
[65] Composition of the Committee:
 a. Members shall be appointed proportionally from recognized blocs in the Assembly;
 b. The Chair shall not be from the same bloc as the sitting President;
 c. At least one seat shall be reserved for opposition parties with no ministerial portfolios.
[66] Judicial safeguards:
 a. Any domestic collection of communications, or intrusive surveillance upon citizens, shall require judicial authorization except in narrowly defined emergency conditions, with:
[67] Post-facto judicial review, and
[68] Mandatory reporting to the Committee.
 b. RNIA shall not maintain detention facilities, nor shall it interrogate detainees except in cooperation with lawful police or relevant authorities.
[70] SECTION 8 – TRANSITIONAL ARRANGEMENTS
[71] Within ninety (90) days of this Act’s entry into force, the government shall:
 a. Present to the Assembly a detailed transition plan for the transfer of assets and personnel from RIA and GRI to RNIA;
 b. Propose the initial Director of RNIA for confirmation.
[72] All existing laws concerning RIA and GRI shall remain in force to the extent they are not inconsistent with this Act until repealed, amended, or replaced.
[73] Any ongoing operations of RIA or GRI at the time this Act enters into force shall be:
 a. Reviewed by the Director-designate of RNIA;
 b. Either:
[74] Transferred to RNIA,
[75] Transferred to the reconstituted RIA, or
[76] Terminated, in accordance with law and national security needs.
[78] SECTION 9 – BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
[79] The RNIA shall have a separate budget line within the national budget, subject to:
 a. Annual approval by the Assembly;
 b. Confidential annexes where necessary for security, with oversight by the Committee.
[80] The reconstituted RIA shall likewise have a distinct budget, clearly separated from RNIA expenditures.
[81] No off-the-books funding, unreported accounts, or unregistered assets shall be permitted for RNIA or the reconstituted RIA. Any such schemes shall constitute criminal offenses under the Ethics & Conflict of Interest Act and related statutes.
[83] SECTION 10 – ENTRY INTO FORCE
[84] This Act shall enter into force upon signature by the President of the Republic and publication in the Official Gazette.
[85] The government shall adopt necessary implementing decrees and regulations within six (6) months of entry into force.

[1] Reunion Broadcasting Daily Network
[2] Special Report — Dalmatia Front Crisis
[3] Dateline: Reunion City | 10 September 1992 | 12:10 PM
[4] The Ministry of Defense confirmed today that Reunion forces in occupied Dalmatia have suffered severe losses following a major Croatian escalation that began with massed rocket artillery and 155mm shelling, followed by armored pressure and a breakthrough in the northwest sector.
[5] Officials say Croatian regular units—supported by UDF militia elements—successfully ruptured the line across the landbridge and pushed south of the lake beyond it, forcing Reunion units to fall back to a secondary defensive line. The withdrawal has effectively split parts of the force, with commanders reporting frayed communications and widespread disorder under sustained fire.
[6] Confirmed Losses (Reunion)
[7] According to the Defense Ministry’s preliminary list of equipment losses as of 11:54 AM, Reunion has lost:
[8] 12 155mm howitzers
[9] 3 AMX-13/90 light tanks
[10] 1 EC-130Q TACAMO aircraft
[11] 1 Mirage 5F, 2 Mirage IIIE, 1 Mirage IIIR
[12] 84 infantry sections (counted in this report as platoon-equivalents in the field returns)
[13] The government emphasized that casualty figures remain provisional while missing personnel are accounted for and scattered units are reassembled.
[14] Casualties (Platoon-based accounting)
[15] Under the Army’s current emergency reporting method—treating each listed infantry “section” loss as a 30-man platoon rendered combat-ineffective—the confirmed platoon-equivalent losses amount to:
[16] 84 platoons × 30 = 2,520 personnel (dead, wounded, missing, or captured)
[17] A senior defense official, speaking on background, described the pattern of losses as consistent with heavy rocket artillery strikes followed by break-ins and local overrun events.
[18] Croatian & UDF Losses (as reported by RNIO field assessment)
[19] Reunion claims significant Croatian losses including:
[20] 18 2A36 Giatsint-B 152mm guns
[21] 18 BM-21 Grad launchers
[22] 4 T-80 tanks
[23] One Croatian jet (MiG-19)
 and multiple infantry and support vehicles. UDF militia elements reportedly lost mortars and armored vehicles.
[24] Political Response
[25] President Donahue has convened an emergency national security session and requested urgent consultations with allied governments. Parliament is expected to be briefed today on emergency appropriations, mobilization measures, and internal security steps.
[26] RBD will continue updates as official casualty notifications and unit status reports are confirmed.

sources.text:
Hard Realism Mode engaged.
No narrative smoothing. No optimism bias. No heroic cushioning.

Below is the structured canonical baseline.

REUNION MASTER POLITICAL — BASELINE v1

Date: October 3rd, 1992

1️⃣ POLITICAL STATE
CURRENT PRESIDENT

Dax Donahue

VICE PRESIDENT
Jack Younger

Party: Unafilliated (Heavy backing from Reform Republican Party (RRP))
Status: Constitutionally legitimate, politically weakened, still operational.

Strengths
Seen as competent under fire (Bern + Dalmatia exit without total collapse).
Avoided massacre at Ploče.
Secured US FMS approval (strategic win).
Maintains functioning executive control over ministries and armed forces.
Weaknesses
Signed territorial concession to Croatia (hawks furious).
Accepted UN hostage corridor (hardliners furious).
Increasing dependence on US (nationalists furious).
Multiple foreign actors possess leverage material.
Parliament is functionally gridlocked.

Executive Control Reality

He still commands:

Armed Forces
RNIA / RNIO
Interior Ministry
Formal emergency authority

He does not command:

Parliament loyalty
Unified coalition backing
Stable domestic legitimacy across classes

Presidential approval (national): 41%

Urban middle class: 45%
Rural conservative: 38%
Veterans: 50%
Dalmatian Territory (post-treaty): 34%

KING ZO III

Status: Constitutional monarch, politically influential, not executive.

Control
Controls significant personal wealth (via Royla + legacy holdings).
Has loyalist networks within:
Officer corps (older generation)
Aristocratic families
Business elite
No direct constitutional command authority. (Brother Henry Steiner runs the special forces however)
Public Support

National: 48%

Rural conservatives: 60%
Urban elites: 52%
Youth / reform bloc: 33%
Dalmatian Croat population: 28%

He is popular as a symbol of strength but feared as a destabilizer.

Reality

He cannot legally remove Donahue.

South of the Adriatic trade lanes
West of the Balkans
North of the Eastern Mediterranean energy routes
East of Italy
Within naval transit distance of:
Greece
Turkey
North Africa
Levant

It has:

Deep natural harbors
Mountainous defensible interior
Limited arable land
Strong maritime tradition

Reunion survives because:
It is hard to conquer and useful to control.

MAJOR CITIES (October 1992)
Reunion City (Capital)
Financial core
Government center
Naval headquarters
Largest population
Major industrial base
Split (Dalmatian hub historically)
Major port
Cultural bridge to Balkans
Industrial shipping
Political flashpoint
Torrental
Old trade capital
Oil staging potential
Historic Venetian conflict site
North Industrial Belt
Heavy manufacturing
Defense industry
Mining and refining

Ploče:
Important port.
Not major urban center.

II. ROMAN–MEDIEVAL ERA
Greek Colonization (Pre-Roman)

Minor Greek colonies established trade outposts.

They did not deeply integrate inland.
They controlled ports and traded metals and timber.

Greek influence:

Maritime commerce culture
Early democratic councils in port towns
Coinage systems

But they never politically unified the island.

Roman Conquest (Early Empire)

Romans absorbed the territory after taking it from fragmented Greek holdings.

What Rome did:

Built road networks (still traceable today)
Constructed fortified hill towns
Integrated island into grain + naval system
Established legal Latin foundation
Created urban municipal culture

Romanization was deep.

Language:
Latin-based dialect roots remain in legal and administrative terms.

Infrastructure:
Stone roads and aqueduct ruins still form backbone of certain corridors.

Reunion identity myth later formed around:
“We are Roman before we are Balkan.”

Byzantine Control (Post-Western Collapse)

After Western Rome fell:
Byzantines took control.

They ruled indirectly.
Heavy taxation.
Military governors.

Cultural shift:
Greek liturgical influence.
Orthodox Christianity influence.

But resentment grew.

The Revolt — Battle of Reunion’s Peak

Local noble leader Discorius unified hill clans.

Byzantine garrison defeated in mountain engagement.

Key structural moment:

This is where the Kingdom of Disco emerges.

Independent monarchy forms.
Strong anti-imperial identity.

Founding myth:
“We bow to no empire.”

III. MEDIEVAL TO EARLY MODERN
Ottoman Expansion Period

Ottomans attempted maritime dominance.

Reunion resisted repeatedly.

Reasons they survived:

Strong navy relative to size.
Mountain interior defensive lines.
Ottoman focus prioritized mainland Balkans.

Reunion wins multiple naval engagements.
Avoids tribute status.

This period creates:
Militarized maritime identity.
Permanent suspicion of eastern empires.

Rise as Trade Power

15th–17th centuries:

Reunion expands influence into Dalmatia.
Controls Split region.
Competes directly with Venice.

Reunion merchants:

Active in Levant trade
Compete in Adriatic grain routes
Operate semi-private naval fleets

Trade empire nearly rivaled Venice at peak.

1689 — Battle of Torrential Bay

Venetians decisively defeat Reunion fleet.

Reunion loses:

Major islands
Overseas holdings
Naval dominance

Turning point.

Reunion shifts from expansionist maritime power to defensive mercantile state.

IV. EARLY MODERN → WW1 → WW2
18th–19th Century

Reunion remains neutral power.
Industrializes slowly.
Develops mining and metallurgy.

No colonial empire.
No global expansion.

Focus:
Survival and trade.

WW1

Reunion sides with Greeks against Ottomans.

Motivation:
Historic rivalry.
Orthodox ties.
Anti-Ottoman legacy.

Reunion navy supports Balkan operations.
Limited land deployment.

Outcome:
Regional prestige boost.
But economically strained.

Interwar Period

King Zo crowned at 16 after father’s death.
Initially popular.
Disciplined.
Reform-minded.

Over time:
Power consolidates.
Opposition suppressed.

ATG emerges.
Political polarization rises.

V. WW2 / CIVIL WAR ERA
1938 — Alignment with Axis

King publicly aligns with Hitler and Mussolini.

Motivation:
Anti-communism.
Geopolitical survival calculation.
Prestige diplomacy.

Domestic backlash severe.

1943–1946 Civil War

ATG launches uprising.
Northern island seized.
Urban warfare brutal.

Dax Donahue’s uncle leads rebels.
Hartmann lineage central.

Civil war:
High casualties.
Economic destruction.
Deep social scars.

Outcome:
Monarchy survives but constitution weakened.
Long memory of ideological fracture.

VI. 1960s – PRESENT (Cold War Era)
Greek War Intervention

Communist uprising in Torrental port.

Reunion intervenes in Greece:
Initial nationalist victories.
Then Soviet VDV + armor deploy.

Reunion pushed back to Evino line.

Massive air losses:
Reunion loses high ratio of aircraft.
Soviets lose far greater raw numbers.

Black Sea Fleet suffers heavy losses.
But Reunion air defense network severely damaged.

Post-Greek War Reality

Military reforms begin.
Radar rebuild.
SAM modernization.
But economy strained.

1980s–1992

Industrial rebuilding.
Defense expansion.
Oil surveys begin.

Yugoslav collapse destabilizes region.
Dalmatian involvement.
Croatian war.
Bosnian extremism.

12-year Croatian treaty signed.
Territory lost south of Split.

Reunion modernizing aggressively.
Balancing:
US
France
Turkey
Serbia
Soviets

STRUCTURAL HISTORICAL TRAITS

Reunion historically:

Survives empires.
Avoids annexation.
Wins defensive wars.
Overreaches in maritime conflicts.
Splits internally under ideological strain.
Rebuilds through trade.

I. DEMOGRAPHIC BREAKDOWN (CORE ISLAND)

Total population: ~19–21 million (core island + retained territories)

Ethnic Composition (Core Island)
Reunionist (Latin-Roman heritage majority) — ~78%
Dalmatian Croat (minority remaining after treaty withdrawal) — ~8%
Greek minority (historic trade families) — ~4%
Serb minority — ~3%
Mixed Balkan minorities — ~4%
Other (Levantine traders, small North African diaspora, etc.) — ~3%

The state is majority Reunionist.
But it is not monoethnic.

II. RELIGIOUS STRUCTURE
Dominant Religion: Roman Catholicism (~72%)

Institutional influence:
Very high socially.
Moderate politically.
Low formally (no state church, but heavy influence).

The Church:

Strong in rural regions.
Influential among veterans.
Cautious about militarism but anti-communist.
Deeply hostile to radical Islamist framing from Bosnia.
Eastern Orthodox (~11%)

Includes:

Greek minority
Serb minority
Some rural holdovers from Byzantine era

Orthodox community:
Quiet.
Politically careful.
Sensitive to Serbian relations.

Secular / nominal Catholic (~12%)

Urban professional class.
Younger demographics.
Less religious intensity.

Muslim minority (~4–5%)

Primarily:

Small Bosniak diaspora
Some migrant communities
Historic Ottoman-era families

Heavily scrutinized post-Bosnian escalation.
No evidence of domestic extremism networks at scale.
But under suspicion socially.

IV. RELIGION & POLITICS

Catholic Church Position:

Publicly calls for peace.
Privately supports strong defense posture.
Opposes extremist Islamist rhetoric from Bosnia.
Does not want dictatorship revival.

Church influence in Parliament:
Indirect but powerful within RCA and rural NSF bloc.

V. ETHNIC TENSIONS
Reunionist Majority

Identity narrative:
“We are Roman before we are Balkan.”

Core traits:

Maritime pride
Anti-imperial mythos
Suspicion of eastern powers
Memory of civil war
Dalmatian Croat Population

After treaty:
Bitterness high.

Viewpoints split:

Older generation: nostalgic for Reunion period.
Younger generation: drifting toward Croatian identity.
Merchant class: pragmatic.

Risk:
If Croatia destabilizes region again, Dalmatian communities become flashpoint.

9️⃣ INTELLIGENCE & INTERNAL SECURITY ARCHITECTURE
I. STRUCTURE OVERVIEW

Reunion’s security system is layered but not fully centralized.

It consists of:

RNIA – Internal Security & Counterintelligence
RNIO – External Intelligence
Military Intelligence Directorate (MID)
Presidential Security Council
Parliamentary Oversight Committee (weak)
Police & Regional Security Bureaus

These entities cooperate — but compete.

II. RNIA

(Reunion National Internal Agency)

Role

Domestic counterintelligence.
Counter-extremism.
Political security monitoring.
Critical infrastructure protection.

Capabilities
Surveillance (legal framework broad under emergency doctrine)
Detention authority
Infiltration of extremist networks
Border security liaison
Strengths
Experienced from civil war era.
Strong Catholic institutional connections.
Deep penetration of nationalist networks.
Weaknesses
Politically distrusted by left and Dalmatian bloc.
Resource stretched.
Old-guard officers remain from monarchist era.
Vulnerable to parliamentary inquiry.
Current Priorities
Monitoring Bosnian diaspora channels.
Tracking Soviet proxy activity.
Monitoring military morale.
Watching radical NSF factions.
Risk

If RNIA is politicized:
Civil trust collapses rapidly.

III. RNIO

(Reunion National Intelligence Office)

Role

Foreign intelligence collection.
Strategic analysis.
Covert foreign operations.

Capabilities
Balkan HUMINT networks.
Maritime surveillance.
Signals intelligence (limited).
Liaison with Serbia quietly.
Limited liaison with France and Turkey.
Strengths
Experienced Balkan operators.
Maritime intelligence depth.
Deep regional knowledge.
Weaknesses
Weak satellite capability (US dependent).
No global intelligence reach.
Limited Arabic world penetration.
Current Priorities
Monitoring Bosnia regime shifts.
Soviet fleet tracking.
Oil maritime disputes.
Watching Greece quietly.
IV. MILITARY INTELLIGENCE DIRECTORATE (MID)
Role

Operational intelligence for armed forces.

Capabilities
Battlefield recon.
Electronic intercept (limited).
Radar integration.
Forward surveillance teams.
Weaknesses
Poor strategic warning redundancy.
Limited airborne ISR (E-3 not delivered).
Vulnerable radar sites.
Concern

If Soviet strike suppresses radar:
MID loses eyes quickly.

V. PRESIDENTIAL SECURITY COUNCIL

Chaired by Donahue.

Members:

Defense Minister
Intelligence heads
Military Chief
Finance Minister (when needed)

Real power center in crises.

VI. PARLIAMENTARY OVERSIGHT

Exists.
Weak.
Politicized.

Used as leverage tool during scandals.

Cannot meaningfully control intelligence day-to-day.

VII. FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE RELATIONSHIPS
United States
Intelligence sharing selective.
US has SIGINT superiority.
End-use monitoring gives US oversight leverage.

US likely has more intelligence on Reunion elites than Reunion has on itself.

France
Professional intelligence cooperation.
Maritime and defense sharing.
Less intrusive than US.
Serbia
Quiet HUMINT exchange.
Tactical information flow.
No formal alliance.
Turkey
Growing relationship.
Mutual monitoring of Greece and USSR.
Greece
Limited cooperation.
Mutual suspicion due to oil overlap.
VIII. BLACKMAIL STRUCTURE

The intelligence community knows:

Bosnia holds material.
US holds material.
Serbia holds partial material.

This creates internal paranoia.

If one leaks:
Intelligence apparatus forced into damage control.

IX. INTERNAL SECURITY PRESSURE POINTS
Dalmatian identity networks.
Monarchist cells.
NSF hardliners.
Radical student factions.
Potential foreign agitation among Muslim minority.
X. COUP RESILIENCE

Military loyalty:
Institutional, not ideological.

Intelligence loyalty:
Divided between constitution and stability.

RNIA unlikely to back unconstitutional coup unless:
Executive collapse occurs.

XI. FOREIGN INTERFERENCE RISK

Most likely actors:

USSR (destabilization, not invasion).
Bosnia (information warfare).
Croatia (legal treaty manipulation).
US (political leverage, not destabilization).
XII. SYSTEM STABILITY ASSESSMENT
Sector	Stability
Domestic intelligence	Stable
Foreign intelligence	Competent but limited
Counterintelligence	Active
Coup resistance	Moderate
Foreign penetration	Present but controlled
Blackmail containment	Fragile
XIII. TRUE RISK

Reunion does not face intelligence collapse.

It faces:
Political miscalculation.

Intelligence services can warn.
They cannot fix reckless political decisions.

Emilios Economic Reform Plans 1992
1. National Infrastructure Spine Program
What it is:
 Multi-year push to fix the core arteries:
Ports: Reunion City, Torrental, one Dalmatian port.


Roads: main industrial and rural spines.


Rail: trunk corridors prepared for electrification, diesel upgrades elsewhere.


Grid: substations and lines to stabilize power for industry and cities.


Status:
Moved through Parliament to presidents desk



2. Lucania Twin-Reactor “Trident” Nuclear Refit
What it is:
Refit and reopen the abandoned twin-reactor Lucania plant with modern safety systems.


Use it as the baseload anchor for electrification and industrial growth in the north.


Linked decision:
Capital nuclear plant in Reunion City is paused. Land and plans reserved, but no new build until Lucania proves the model.


Status:
Moving forward. Policy line agreed: pause capital plant, prioritize Lucania refit. Detailed engineering and financing planning underway.



3. Rural Modernization & Food Security Act (RMFS) – Draft Bill
What it is:
Equipment modernization grants + cheap credit for farmers.


Region-specific crop subsidies with “insurance” style reimbursements if harvests fail.


State purchase of surplus crops for strategic reserves and school/military supply.


Co-ops and storage (silos, cold chain) to cut waste and strengthen bargaining power.


Status:
Needs further planning.


Internally drafted with Agriculture, not introduced in Parliament yet.


Next steps: quiet consultations with farmers’ unions, co-ops, LUP, rural MPs before it goes public.



4. Land Tenure & Rural Property Modernization (Land Reform)
What it is:
National cadastre and title cleanup (starting in Lucania, Northern Island, Torrental hinterland).


Incentives for voluntary consolidation/co-ops (scale without forced seizures).


Tax pressure + incentives to force big underused estates to either modernize or partner with tenants.


Status:
Concept / white paper stage.


Emilio has asked Agriculture to work with him; no bill text yet.


This will be politically explosive if rushed – it needs precise legal work and a long rollout plan.



5. Rail Modernization & HS Trunk Line
What it is:
Kill steam across the network.


High-speed electric corridor:
 Lucania → Steinberg → Reunion City → Torrental (southern capital)
 – prioritized for speed, reliability, and affordable mass transport.


Diesel mainline/branch upgrades everywhere else (northern rural lines, Torrental hinterland, Dalmatia, fringe islands).


Status:
Strategic plan in development.


Political direction is set (this is the model).


Needs a formal 10-year National Rail Modernization Plan: exact km, costs per phase, contractor mix, and tie-in with Lucania grid timeline.



6. Government Expenditure Audit & Cuts (Confidential)
What it is:
Full audit of state spending to find:


Dead security programs and wartime leftovers.


Zombie SOEs and pointless subsidies.


Vanity projects and overlapping ministries.


Goal: free 2–4% of the budget over a few years to fund the infrastructure, nuclear, and rural programs without blowing the deficit sky-high.


Status:
Underway / For President’s eyes only.


Emilio has ordered it; Finance + audit bodies are compiling.


Output will be a confidential cut list for Donahue, then a public-facing “reform” package after they decide what to kill.

1946 CONSTITUTION – OUTLINE
1. Preamble & Foundational Principles
Adopted after the 1930s civil war and the collapse of the old absolute monarchy.
Core ideas:
Reunion is a democratic republic built to prevent:


One-party rule,


Military dictatorship,


Absolute monarchy returning.


It acknowledges:


The “historic role of the Crown” and keeps the King as a symbolic Head of State,


But vests real power in elected institutions.


No one’s touched the text since 1946; all the bending has been done via ordinary laws and “interpretation.”

2. Article I – The State & Institutions
Form of State
“Unitary, indivisible Republic of Reunion.”


Islands (Northern / Central / Southern / Dalmatia / fringe islands) recognized as administrative regions, not full federal units.


The monarchy is described as a “hereditary Crown within the Republic, guardian of continuity and dignity of the State.”


Separation of Powers
Legislative: Assembly of the Republic (unicameral).


Executive: President of the Republic + Council of Ministers.


Judiciary: independent courts, plus a Constitutional Court.


Outdated part:
 Text still references a “President of the Council of Ministers” as if there’s a Prime Minister, but in practice that role has fused into the Presidency by statute and custom. The constitution was never updated to reflect that.

3. Article II – Rights & Duties of Citizens
This is your de-facto “bill of rights.” It’s noble and also shot through with 1940s paranoia.
Citizenship
Jus sanguinis as default:


Child of a Reunionist citizen is a citizen.


Jus soli only for:


Children born on Reunion soil to stateless parents or unknown parentage.


Naturalization:


Left to statute (see Immigration Code below).


Equality Clause
“All citizens are equal before the law without distinction of origin, creed, or political conviction.”


Then a nasty fudge line:


“The law may provide distinctions where required to protect public order, public morals, or the national character.”


That “national character” phrase is a legal cancer – it justifies all sorts of abuse.
Fundamental Rights
Textually guaranteed:
Freedom of expression, press, and opinion.


Freedom of assembly and association.


Freedom of religion and conscience.


Inviolability of the home and correspondence.


Right to due process and defense in criminal matters.


Right to vote and stand for office at age 18.


But all of them are subject to a familiar carve-out:
 “except as limited by law in the interests of security, public order, and the protection of the democratic and republican order.”
That’s the hole every government has driven a truck through.
Duties
Pay taxes.


Serve in the defense of the Republic (basis for conscription law).


Respect the Constitution and “democratic institutions.”



4. Article III – Executive Power
President of the Republic
Election:


Direct popular vote.


Term: 4 years.


Re-election:


No limit to terms


Non-consecutive terms allowed (hence multiple Hartmann-party presidents across decades).


Powers:


Appoints and dismisses ministers and the “President of the Council” (Prime Minister in theory, merged into President in practice).


Promulgates laws; can send a bill back once for reconsideration.


Can call referendums on major constitutional/political issues.


Supreme Commander of Armed Forces.


Can declare a State of Emergency (see Article IV).


May dissolve the Assembly once per term lasting a duration of 3 months with additional extensions granted of up to 6 month extensions at a time. new elections will be held for parliament.


The constitution never codified the current “no Prime Minister” reality. Legally, a hostile Assembly could try to argue parts of the executive architecture are unconstitutional.
The King
Symbolic Head of State:


Signs treaties ceremonially.


Delivers annual “Address to the Nation.”


Has the right to be consulted, to counsel, and to warn.


Reserve powers (vaguely drafted):


In “grave constitutional crisis,” the King may:


Appeal directly to the people,


Request the Assembly to reconsider legislation that, in his view, “gravely harms the constitutional order”.


All of this requires countersignature from the President or a Minister to be valid, but the text is hazy enough that royalists and republicans can both spin it.

5. Article IV – Legislature
Assembly of the Republic
Originally 200 members, elected every 4 years.


Constitution text: “The Assembly shall consist of no fewer than 150 and no more than 300 deputies.”


You recently expanded to 400 seats by statute – strictly speaking, that’s constitutionally dubious. Halvik knows it; everyone decided not to open that can of worms… yet.


Electoral system:


Proportional representation, multi-member constituencies by island/region.


Parties must respect “democratic principles”; openly anti-democratic parties may be banned by law.


Powers:


Passes ordinary laws, budget, taxes.


Can impeach the President (2/3 majority) for “high crimes and grave violations of the Constitution.”


Confirms key appointments (Constitutional Court, some judges, RNIA Director under new statute).



6. Article V – Judiciary
Guarantees judicial independence “subject only to the Constitution and the law.”


Constitutional Court
9 judges.


Appointed by:


President (3),


Assembly (3),


King (3).


12-year non-renewable terms.


Powers:


Review laws for constitutionality.


Rule on disputes between state organs.


Rule on party bans and some electoral disputes.


In practice, appointments have been heavily politicized; this Court has been more cautious than assertive.
Ordinary Courts
Supreme Court of Cassation at the top.


Regional courts and local courts under it.



7. Article VI – Emergency & Security Provisions
President can declare a State of Emergency:


Initially for up to 90 days.


Must be notified to Assembly within 24 hours.


Assembly can approve, modify, or revoke by simple majority.


Under emergency:


Freedom of assembly and strike may be suspended.


Curfews imposed.


Extended detention without charge up to 30 days.


Military and RIA can be deployed internally under special rules.


This is the legal basis for the communist crackdowns, the martial law in Reunion City after the Parliament attack, etc.
No modern safeguards – no explicit prohibition on torture, no explicit ban on blanket censorship.

8. Article VII – Amendments
Amendments require:


2/3 majority in the Assembly.


A second 2/3 vote at least six months later.


Countersignature by President and King.


Optional referendum if 1/3 of Assembly or President requests it.


Threshold is so high that everyone has preferred to work around the constitution instead of updating it. That’s why it’s still half-1946, half-ad hoc practice.

II. KEY LAWS – OUTLINE
Now, the main legal pillars sitting on top of that constitution, shaped by your presidential list:
1. Electoral & Parties Law
Electoral Law of 1952, revised 1968, 1981:


Establishes PR system, seat allocation, thresholds.


Parties must register and accept constitutional order.


Party bans allowed for:


Advocating violent overthrow,


Explicitly anti-democratic ideologies.


Parties & Campaign Finance Act (1981):


Regulates donations, public funding.


Very weak enforcement until recently; lots of loopholes oligarchs and factions exploit.



2. Immigration & Nationality Framework
Primarily:
Immigration & Nationality Code of 1971


Amended 1983 (post-Hartmann leftist era) and 1990 (in response to Greek and Balkan instability).


Key points:
Entry & Residence:
Visa regime with:


Preference for:


Reunion diaspora,


Skilled workers,


Investors.


Broad discretion to deny entry for:


“Threats to the constitutional order,”


National security,


Serious criminal record.


This has historically been used to keep out both foreign communists and foreign right-wing militants.
Naturalization:
Standard path:


10 years legal residence.


Language and civic test.


Clean criminal record.


Demonstrated “integration into Reunion society.”


Diaspora / ethnic-return path:


3–5 years residence, test may be waived.


Designed to bring back Reunionists or their descendants.


Asylum / Refugees:
1990 Asylum Law brought in:


Narrow asylum grounds.


Very high bar for proof.


Broad discretion for Interior and Security to deny on “security” grounds.


This is all very 20th-century – restrictive, opaque, and ripe for abuse. It also has basically no modern framework for long-term migrant integration.

3. Freedom of Expression, Press & Public Order
Grounded in several acts:
Public Order & Social Peace Act (1950)


Bans “organizations advocating the violent overthrow of the constitutional order.”


Allows authorities to ban demonstrations if they “threaten public peace or constitutional values.”


Press & Broadcast Act (1962)


Licensing for broadcast media.


Defamation criminalized.


“Insulting the Crown or the Republic’s institutions” is a criminal offence.


Vague “offence to public morals” clause allows censorship.


National Security & Subversive Activities Act (1977) (Hartmann-era, leftist security obsessions):


Criminalizes:


“Propaganda in service of a foreign power hostile to the Republic.”


“Apology for political violence.”


Used primarily against communists in Torrental protests, but on paper it’s ideology-agnostic.


De jure, free speech exists. De facto:
The state has wide latitude to ban gatherings and speech that it deems:


“Subversive,”


“Anti-constitutional,” or


“Morally harmful.”


Halvik, if he wants a freer modern state, has to either:
Reform these laws, or


Push constitutional court challenges against their vaguer parts.



4. Term Limits & Presidency in Law
Beyond the Constitution:
Presidential Elections Act (1951)


Clarifies:


4-year term.


Two consecutive terms maximum per individual.


Non-consecutive terms allowed.


Provides:


If the President dies or resigns:


The Speaker of the Assembly becomes Acting President until elections in 90 days.


There’s no statutory recall mechanism; only impeachment (2/3 Assembly) and elections. That’s why Strevo stepping down after his stroke requires a political, not legal, process.

5. Defense, RIA/RNIA & Internal Security
Defense & Armed Forces Act (1963)


Codifies civilian control; conscription; structure of army, navy, air force.


RIA Statute (1969)


Created RIA as hybrid internal security + intelligence organ.


Granted broad powers under emergency conditions:


Surveillance,


Detention handoff,


Internal ops.


RNIA Reorganization Act (1992)


Your new law:


Creates RNIA as a separate, civilian intel agency.


Strips RIA of formal intel analysis role; redefines it as a national-guard-like security force.


Adds parliamentary oversight and a 3/5 confirmation rule for RNIA Director.


The Constitution hasn’t been updated to reflect this dual structure; it still speaks vaguely of “security organs.”



6. Criminal Code & Procedure
Still largely based on:
Penal Code 1948, heavily amended but structurally old.


Code of Criminal Procedure 1954.


Problems:
Outdated offences remain:


“Insult to foreign heads of state.”


Broad “offence to public morals.”


“Subversive assembly” with vague wording.


Procedural issues:


Pre-trial detention rules were written with internal wars and political violence in mind; authorities can hold suspects longer than most modern European systems.


Weak protection of the right to counsel during the first 24–48 hours of detention, especially under emergency laws.


If Halvik wants to modernize justice, this is a prime target.

7. Labor, Unions & Strikes
Labor Relations Act (1960) and Trade Union Act (1974):


Recognize unions and the right to strike.


But:


Strikes can be banned in a wide range of “essential services.”


Emergency laws let the state suspend strikes at will.
